fields.title: Clothed with Strength and Dignity
fields.description: Clothed with Strength and Dignity is a heartfelt guide for Christian women in Uganda and East Africa who desire to walk closely with God. Rooted in Scripture and filled with wisdom, prayer, and practical encouragement, this book explores identity in Christ, prayer, marriage, motherhood, service, and Godly living.

fields.title: Rooted in Christ: Your True Identity
fields.body_html:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." Genesis 1:27 (KJV) Before we can talk about what a Christian woman does, we must first understand who she is. So much confusion in our lives comes from forgetting our true identity. When a woman does not know who she is in Christ, she will try to find her worth in her husband, her children, her education, her beauty, her job, or what other people say about her. Every one of these things can be taken away in a moment. But the identity God gives you can never be taken away.

The Bible teaches us three great truths about who you are. First, you are made in the image of God.

Second, you are redeemed by the blood of Jesus Christ. Third, you are filled with the Holy Spirit and set apart for good works prepared by God Himself.

Consider the first truth. In Genesis 1, when God made the world, He spoke the stars into being, He filled the seas with fish and the skies with birds, He formed the beasts of the field. But when He came to make humanity, He did something different. He said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." And then the text says clearly that He made them male and female, both in His image. This means that as a woman, you are not a lesser reflection of God. You are a full image-bearer of the Living God. Your mind, your emotions, your will, your capacity to love, to create, to reason, to worship — all of these come from God and reflect something of His nature.

The second truth is that you are redeemed. The fall of Adam and Eve brought sin and death into the world, and all of us have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. But God in His mercy sent His only Son, Jesus Christ, who was born of a woman, who lived a perfect life, who died on the cross for our sins, and who rose again on the third day. When you put your faith in Jesus, your sins are washed away. You are no longer condemned. You are adopted into the family of God. The Bible says that as many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God.

Think about what this means. You are a daughter of the King of kings. The same God who made the mountains of Rwenzori, who spread the waters of Lake Victoria, who hung every star in the sky — this God calls you His daughter. The apostle Paul writes that we are heirs of God and joint heirs with Christ. Whatever your earthly situation may be, whether you live in a small house with a leaking roof or a large home in the city, your true inheritance is in heaven, and it is far greater than anything this world can offer.

The third truth is that you have the Holy Spirit living within you. When you came to Christ, God did not leave you to try to live the Christian life by your own strength. He gave you His Spirit, who comforts you, teaches you, convicts you of sin, and empowers you to live a holy life. The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you. You are not weak. You are filled with the mighty power of God.

Let me show you this truth through the life of one woman in the Bible. In the Gospel of John, chapter four, we read about a woman of Samaria. She came to the well in the heat of the day, probably because she was ashamed to come when the other women came in the morning. She had been married five times, and the man she was with now was not her husband. Her life was broken.

Her identity was built on relationships that kept failing her. But Jesus met her at the well. He knew everything about her, and yet He did not condemn her. He offered her living water. He told her who the true Messiah was. And she ran back to her village and told everyone, "Come, see a man who told me all things that ever I did." Many believed because of her testimony. That same woman, who had hidden from her neighbors in shame, became the first evangelist to her village. Jesus changed her identity.

Or consider Mary Magdalene. Scripture tells us that Jesus cast seven demons out of her. Before meeting Jesus, she was tormented. After meeting Jesus, she followed Him, supported His ministry, stood at the cross when most of the disciples had fled, and was the first person to see the risen Lord on Easter morning. The One who knew her fully is the One who gave her a new name and a new calling.

In the history of the Church, we see this same truth lived out beautifully. Consider Perpetua, a young North African woman who lived around the year 200 AD. She was only twenty-two years old, a new mother with a baby still at her breast, when she was arrested for being a Christian. Her father pleaded with her to renounce her faith and save her life. She refused.

She wrote a diary from prison that survives to this day. In it, she recorded that she knew who she was — a handmaid of Jesus Christ. That identity was stronger than her father's tears, stronger than her love for her own child, stronger than the fear of death. She went to the arena singing psalms and died for her Lord. The early Church remembered her name for centuries. Her identity in Christ gave her strength that nothing could take away.

My sister, what is your identity built on today? If it is built on your appearance, it will fade. If it is built on what your husband says about you, he is only a man and may fail you. If it is built on whether your children succeed, they are still sinners who may grieve your heart. If it is built on what your neighbors think, they will judge you by standards that change. Only Christ is the Rock.

Only in Him is your identity unshakable.

Take some time this week to meditate on who you are in Christ. Write down these truths. Say them out loud. You might say, "I am a daughter of God. I am made in His image. I am redeemed by the blood of Jesus. I am filled with the Holy Spirit. I am loved with an everlasting love. Nothing can separate me from the love of God in Christ Jesus my Lord." When the enemy whispers lies to you, answer him with the truth of God's word.

A Prayer Heavenly Father, I thank You that You made me in Your image. I thank You that You sent Your Son Jesus to die for my sins and to make me Your daughter. I thank You that Your Spirit lives within me. Forgive me for the times I have built my identity on things that do not last. Teach me today to know who I am in You. Give me the courage to walk in that truth, so that I may glorify You in all I do. In the name of Jesus Christ, my Lord and Saviour, Amen.

fields.title: The Mighty Ministry of Prayer
fields.body_html:
"Pray without ceasing." 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (KJV) Of all the works the Christian woman can do, there is none more powerful than prayer. A woman on her knees can change history. She can bring down strongholds of the enemy. She can move the hand of God to heal, to save, to provide, and to protect. Kingdoms have risen and fallen because of praying women. Entire families have been brought to Christ through the faithful, secret prayers of a mother or a grandmother. Do not ever think of prayer as small work.

The Bible gives us clear instructions about prayer. We are to pray without ceasing. We are to pray for our enemies and those who persecute us. We are to pray for kings and all those in authority, that we may lead quiet and peaceable lives. We are to pray for one another that we may be healed.

We are to pray in secret, and our Father who sees in secret will reward us openly. We are to pray with faith, not doubting. We are to pray in the name of Jesus. And we are to pray in the power of the Holy Spirit.

Let me introduce you to Hannah. Her story is in First Samuel chapter one. Hannah was married to a man named Elkanah, but she could not bear children. In that culture, this was a great shame and sorrow. The other wife, Peninnah, mocked her for it. Year after year, Hannah went up to the tabernacle of the Lord at Shiloh, and year after year she wept. One day, her prayer changed everything. She went into the house of the Lord and poured out her heart. She prayed so deeply that her lips moved but no sound came out. Eli the priest thought she was drunk, but she was not drunk with wine — she was drunk with sorrow and desperation for God to hear her. She made a vow: if God would give her a son, she would dedicate him to the Lord all the days of his life.

God heard Hannah. She conceived and gave birth to Samuel. And Samuel grew up to become one of the greatest prophets in the history of Israel. He anointed King David, the man after God's own heart, whose descendant was Jesus the Messiah. Think about that, sister.

The whole line of King David, leading to the birth of our Saviour, came through the answered prayer of a weeping woman. Never despise your tears before the Lord.

Then there was Anna, in Luke chapter two. She was an old woman, a widow of more than sixty years by the time we meet her. The scripture says she did not depart from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day. When Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple, Anna saw Him, recognized who He was, and gave thanks. Her years of prayer prepared her to recognize the Messiah the moment He arrived. Prayer trains your eyes to see what others cannot see.

The Lord Jesus Himself taught us how to pray. He taught us to begin with worship — "Hallowed be thy name." He taught us to pray for God's will — "Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done." He taught us to ask for our daily needs — "Give us this day our daily bread." He taught us to seek forgiveness and to forgive others. He taught us to ask for protection from temptation and deliverance from evil. Every time you say the Lord's Prayer, you are praying a prayer that Jesus Himself gave to us.

In the history of the Church, there is perhaps no more famous praying mother than Monica. She was the mother of Augustine, who became one of the greatest teachers the Church has ever known.

But before Augustine became a man of God, he was a rebel. He chased worldly pleasures, he followed false teachers, he broke his mother's heart again and again. Monica prayed for him for many years — some say almost thirty years. She wept for him. She followed him from North Africa to Italy. She would not give up. One day, Augustine heard a child's voice saying, "Take and read, take and read." He opened the scriptures, read a passage from Romans, and gave his life to Christ. He later wrote that he owed his salvation to the tears of his mother. My sister, if you are praying for a wayward son or daughter, or a husband who does not yet know the Lord, do not give up. Monica prayed for thirty years. Your prayers are not wasted.

Closer to our own time and place, the East African Revival of the 1930s and the following decades was born in prayer. In the hills of Rwanda, in Uganda, in Kenya, small groups of Christians began to meet and pray with great earnestness. They confessed their sins to one another. They walked in the light. And the Spirit of God fell upon them. The revival spread to Tanzania, to the Congo, and around the world. Women played a central role in this movement. They prayed in their homes, they witnessed in the markets, they formed fellowships that still exist today. The fire of that revival came down because women and men were willing to pray.

So how do you develop a life of prayer? Let me suggest a few simple steps. First, choose a time.

It does not have to be a long time at first. Five minutes in the early morning, before the children wake, is a good start. As your prayer life grows, you will want more time with the Lord, not less.

Second, choose a place. Jesus said to enter into your closet, meaning a private place. Perhaps it is a corner of your bedroom, a seat under a tree, or a place in the garden. Third, use a simple structure.

You might begin with thanksgiving, then confession of sin, then intercession for others, then your own requests. Fourth, pray the scriptures. Open your Bible to the Psalms or to the prayers of Paul in Ephesians or Colossians and pray them back to God. Fifth, keep a prayer list. Write down the names of your husband, your children, your pastor, your neighbors, your president, the missionaries, the lost. Pray through that list regularly. Sixth, pray throughout the day. While cooking, while washing, while walking to the garden, lift your heart to the Lord.

Do not be discouraged when you do not see immediate answers. God's timing is not our timing.

Sometimes He answers the moment we ask. Sometimes He waits. Sometimes He answers in ways we did not expect. But He always hears. The prayer of a righteous woman avails much.

A Prayer Lord Jesus, teach me to pray. I confess that I am often too busy, too distracted, too tired to come before Your throne. Forgive me. Draw me back to the secret place. Give me the heart of Hannah, who poured out her soul before You. Give me the faith of Anna, who watched and waited for the Messiah. Make me a woman of prayer, that my family, my church, my nation, and my generation may be blessed because I bent my knees before You. In Your mighty name I pray, Amen.

fields.title: Hiding God's Word in Your Heart
fields.body_html:
"Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." Psalm 119:11 (KJV) If prayer is the breath of the Christian woman, the word of God is her daily food. Our Lord Jesus said that man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. You would not consider going without food for days at a time — you would grow weak and ill. And yet how many Christian women go day after day, week after week, without reading, hearing, or meditating on the scriptures? Is it any wonder that we feel spiritually weak, confused, and tossed about by every trouble?

The Bible is not an ordinary book. It was written over a period of about fifteen hundred years by more than forty different human authors, in three languages, on three continents. And yet it has one great message and one great Author — the Holy Spirit of God. Every word of it is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness. When you read the Bible, you are hearing the very voice of God speaking to you.

For thousands of years, most believers could not read the scriptures for themselves. They were copied by hand, and a single copy of the Bible could cost more than a family earned in a year.

When the printing press was invented in Europe in the 1400s, and when the Bible began to be translated into common languages, it changed the world. And now, here in East Africa, we have the Bible in many of our own languages — Luganda, Swahili, Kinyarwanda, Runyankole, Luo, and many more. What a gift this is. Do not take it for granted. There are women in other parts of the world today who walk for hours to find a single copy of the scriptures.

The Bible tells us of women who loved the word of God. Mary, the mother of Jesus, when she heard the message of the angel Gabriel, responded with a song that we now call the Magnificat. If you read it carefully, you will see that almost every line is a quotation or a reference to the Old Testament scriptures. Mary was a young woman, perhaps only fifteen or sixteen years old, and she knew her Bible so well that when she was filled with the Holy Spirit, the word of God flowed out of her as praise. Scripture tells us that Mary kept all these things and pondered them in her heart.

She was a woman who meditated on God's word.

The apostle Paul wrote a letter to his young helper Timothy and reminded him of the faith that dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and in his mother Eunice. He said that from a child Timothy had known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make one wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. Who taught Timothy the scriptures as a child? His mother and his grandmother. They did not wait for him to grow up. They did not say, "When he is older, we will send him to Bible school." They started teaching him when he was a small boy. And the result was that Timothy became one of the great pastors of the early Church and a beloved companion of the apostle Paul.

In the book of Acts, chapter seventeen, the apostles came to a place called Berea. The Bereans were called more noble than those of Thessalonica because they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily to see whether the things Paul preached were so. Notice — they did not just accept what Paul said because he was an apostle. They checked it against the Bible. This is a good example for us. We live in a time when many voices are teaching things that sound good but are not true to the word of God. The safest thing you can do is to know your Bible so well that when a false teacher speaks, you can say in your heart, "That does not match what the scriptures teach."

Now let me speak practically. How do you become a woman of the Word? Let me give you six simple habits.

First, read the Bible daily. Start with ten or fifteen minutes a day. Read through a book of the Bible from beginning to end. The Gospel of Mark is a good place to start because it is short and full of action. Then read John for its depth. Read Genesis to understand the beginning. Read Psalms for prayer and praise. Read Proverbs — one chapter a day, matching the day of the month — for wisdom for daily life.

Second, memorize scripture. Start with one verse a week. Write it on a small paper and carry it in your pocket. Read it when you are cooking, when you are walking, when you are resting. By the end of a year you will have fifty-two verses hidden in your heart.

Psalm 119:11 says, "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee."

Memorized scripture is a weapon against temptation. When the enemy whispers in your ear, you can strike him down with the sword of the Spirit.

Third, meditate on what you read. To meditate means to think deeply, to chew on, to turn the verse over and over in your mind. Ask questions of the text. What does this tell me about God? What does this tell me about myself? Is there a promise to claim? Is there a command to obey? Is there a sin to avoid? Is there an example to follow?

Fourth, study the Bible with other women. Gather together — perhaps a few of you in your church or neighborhood — and read through a book of the Bible. Discuss what you have learned. Pray together. This kind of fellowship strengthens everyone.

Fifth, sit under good teaching. Attend a Bible-believing church where the scriptures are preached faithfully. Listen carefully to the sermons. Take notes if you can read and write. If there are sound radio programs or recordings from trusted preachers in your area, use them wisely.

Sixth, teach others what you learn. There is no better way to understand the Bible than to teach it to someone else, even a child. When you explain a verse to your son or daughter, you will often find that God teaches you even more deeply than before.

Let me close this chapter with some verses that every Christian woman should know by heart.

Write them down. Learn them this year. John 3:16. Romans 8:28. Psalm 23. Proverbs 3:5 and 6.

Proverbs 31:30. Isaiah 41:10. Philippians 4:6 and 7. Philippians 4:13. Second Timothy 3:16 and 17. Galatians 5:22 and 23. The Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6. The Great Commission in Matthew 28:19 and 20. These will be a lamp to your feet and a light to your path all the days of your life.

A Prayer Father in heaven, I thank You that You have given us Your holy Word. Forgive me for the times I have neglected it. Give me a hunger for the scriptures, a hunger greater than my hunger for food. Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things out of Your law. Hide Your word deep in my heart, that I may not sin against You.

Make me a woman who loves Your Word, who lives by Your Word, and who teaches Your Word to the next generation. In Jesus' name, Amen.

You would not consider going without food for days at a time — you would grow weak and ill. And yet how many Christian women go day after day, week after week, without reading, hearing, or meditating on the scriptures? Is it any wonder that we feel spiritually weak, confused, and tossed about by every trouble? The Bible is not an ordinary book. It was written over a period of about fifteen hundred years by more than forty different human authors, in three languages, on three continents. And yet it has one great message and one great Author — the Holy Spirit of God. Every word of it is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness. When you read the Bible, you are hearing the very voice of God speaking to you. For thousands of years, most believers could not read the scriptures for themselves. They were copied by hand, and a single copy of the Bible could cost more than a family earned in a year. When the printing press was invented in Europe in the 1400s, and when the Bible began to be translated into common languages, it changed the world. And now, here in East Africa, we have the Bible in many of our own languages — Luganda, Swahili, Kinyarwanda, Runyankole, Luo, and many more. What a gift this is. Do not take it for granted. There are women in other parts of the world today who walk for hours to find a single copy of the scriptures. The Bible tells us of women who loved the word of God. Mary, the mother of Jesus, when she heard the message of the angel Gabriel, responded with a song that we now call the Magnificat. If you read it carefully, you will see that almost every line is a quotation or a reference to the Old Testament scriptures. Mary was a young woman, perhaps only fifteen or sixteen years old, and she knew her Bible so well that when she was filled with the Holy Spirit, the word of God flowed out of her as praise. Scripture tells us that Mary kept all these things and pondered them in her heart. She was a woman who meditated on God's word. The apostle Paul wrote a letter to his young helper Timothy and reminded him of the faith that dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and in his mother Eunice. He said that from a child Timothy had known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make one wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. Who taught Timothy the scriptures as a child? His mother and his grandmother. They did not wait for him to grow up. They did not say, "When he is older, we will send him to Bible school." They started teaching him when he was a small boy. And the result was that Timothy became one of the great pastors of the early Church and a beloved companion of the apostle Paul. In the book of Acts, chapter seventeen, the apostles came to a place called Berea. The Bereans were called more noble than those of Thessalonica because they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily to see whether the things Paul preached were so. Notice — they did not just accept what Paul said because he was an apostle. They checked it against the Bible. This is a good example for us. We live in a time when many voices are teaching things that sound good but are not true to the word of God. The safest thing you can do is to know your Bible so well that when a false teacher speaks, you can say in your heart, "That does not match what the scriptures teach." Now let me speak practically. How do you become a woman of the Word? Let me give you six simple habits. First, read the Bible daily. Start with ten or fifteen minutes a day. Read through a book of the Bible from beginning to end. The Gospel of Mark is a good place to start because it is short and full of action. Then read John for its depth. Read Genesis to understand the beginning. Read Psalms for prayer and praise. Read Proverbs — one chapter a day, matching the day of the month — for wisdom for daily life. Second, memorize scripture. Start with one verse a week. Write it on a small paper and carry it in your pocket. Read it when you are cooking, when you are walking, when you are resting. By the end of a year you will have fifty-two verses hidden in your heart. Psalm 119:11 says, "Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee." Memorized scripture is a weapon against temptation. When the enemy whispers in your ear, you can strike him down with the sword of the Spirit. Third, meditate on what you read. To meditate means to think deeply, to chew on, to turn the verse over and over in your mind. Ask questions of the text. What does this tell me about God? What does this tell me about myself? Is there a promise to claim? Is there a command to obey? Is there a sin to avoid? Is there an example to follow? Fourth, study the Bible with other women. Gather together — perhaps a few of you in your church or neighborhood — and read through a book of the Bible. Discuss what you have learned. Pray together. This kind of fellowship strengthens everyone. Fifth, sit under good teaching. Attend a Bible-believing church where the scriptures are preached faithfully. Listen carefully to the sermons. Take notes if you can read and write. If there are sound radio programs or recordings from trusted preachers in your area, use them wisely. Sixth, teach others what you learn. There is no better way to understand the Bible than to teach it to someone else, even a child. When you explain a verse to your son or daughter, you will often find that God teaches you even more deeply than before. Let me close this chapter with some verses that every Christian woman should know by heart. Write them down. Learn them this year. John 3:16. Romans 8:28. Psalm 23. Proverbs 3:5 and 6. Proverbs 31:30. Isaiah 41:10. Philippians 4:6 and 7. Philippians 4:13. Second Timothy 3:16 and 17. Galatians 5:22 and 23. The Lord's Prayer in Matthew 6. The Great Commission in Matthew 28:19 and 20. These will be a lamp to your feet and a light to your path all the days of your life. A Prayer Father in heaven, I thank You that You have given us Your holy Word. Forgive me for the times I have neglected it. Give me a hunger for the scriptures, a hunger greater than my hunger for food. Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things out of Your law. Hide Your word deep in my heart, that I may not sin against You. Make me a woman who loves Your Word, who lives by Your Word, and who teaches Your Word to the next generation. In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: Loving and Respecting Your Husband
fields.body_html:
"Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband." Ephesians 5:33 (KJV) Marriage was God's idea. Before there was sin, before there was any sorrow in the world, God said it was not good for the man to be alone, and He made a woman to be his helper and companion.

The very first wedding was performed by God Himself in the Garden of Eden. This tells us something very important. Marriage is not a human invention. It is a sacred covenant designed by God, and it reflects something of His own nature — the love between Christ and His Church.

In our time, marriage is under great attack. Some say it is old-fashioned. Some say it is a prison for women. Some say it should be ended as soon as it becomes hard. Others treat it as a contract that can be broken when either party is unsatisfied. But my sister, the Bible gives us a very different picture. Marriage is meant to last a lifetime. It is meant to be a place of love, respect, companionship, faithfulness, and fruitfulness. And within marriage, God has given the Christian wife a beautiful and powerful calling.

The apostle Paul writes in Ephesians chapter five that wives should submit to their own husbands as to the Lord, and that husbands should love their wives as Christ loved the Church and gave Himself for her. These two commands go together. A husband is not a king who rules harshly. He is called to sacrificial love. A wife is not a slave. She is called to willing and loving support of her husband's leadership. When both the husband and the wife obey the Lord in their different callings, a marriage becomes a picture of the gospel itself.

Peter writes something beautiful in First Peter chapter three. He speaks to wives, and he uses Sarah as an example. Sarah called Abraham lord, and she obeyed him. Peter tells Christian wives that their beauty should not come mainly from braided hair, or gold jewelry, or fine clothing, but from the hidden person of the heart — a meek and quiet spirit — which is in the sight of God of great price. This does not mean a Christian wife must never speak or have thoughts of her own.

Sarah spoke her mind to Abraham. Abigail spoke her mind to David. The Proverbs 31 wife opens her mouth with wisdom. What Peter means is that the Christian wife is not loud, not contentious, not sharp-tongued, not always fighting for her own way. She carries herself with dignity. Her spirit is calm. And even unbelieving husbands can be won by the conduct of their wives without a word.

Consider Priscilla in the book of Acts. She was married to Aquila, and they worked together as tentmakers. They traveled with Paul. They opened their home to the church. When they heard the eloquent preacher Apollos, who did not yet fully understand the gospel, they took him aside together and explained the way of God more accurately. Priscilla is almost always mentioned alongside her husband — sometimes her name is even listed first — and they served the Lord together as a team. This is a beautiful picture of Christian marriage. Husband and wife, working shoulder to shoulder for the Kingdom.

Or consider Ruth. When Boaz saw her, he did not fall in love first because of her beauty. He fell in love because of her character. Her kindness to Naomi, her hard work in the fields, her willingness to follow the God of Israel — these things made her stand out. Boaz said to her that all the city knew she was a virtuous woman. Long before she was married, Ruth was already living like a godly wife.

Let me speak practically, because theory without practice does not help anyone. How can you love and respect your husband this week?

Speak well of him. Do not join the women at the market or the well who run down their husbands.

When he is away, let your words about him build him up. Children especially are listening. Never tear down their father in front of them. If he has faults — and all husbands have faults, just as all wives do — take those faults to God in prayer, not to the gossips of the village.

Listen to him. When he comes home tired from work, do not immediately load him with every problem the children made that day. Let him sit. Bring him a cup of tea. Ask him about his day.

Many husbands are starving for a wife who will actually listen to them.

Care for yourself and your home. Keep yourself clean and modest. Keep your home orderly. A husband who enjoys coming home is a husband who stays home. This does not mean you must be perfect — no one is. It means that you do your part to make your home a peaceful, welcoming place.

Be faithful to him in body and in heart. Do not flirt with other men. Do not compare your husband to other men. Do not entertain fantasies from movies or novels. Guard your heart, for out of it are the issues of life.

Pray for him every day. Pray for his work, his health, his spiritual walk, his decisions, his temptations. A husband who is prayed for is a blessed man, even if he does not know why things are going well for him.

Now let me address a hard situation. What if your husband is not yet a Christian? What if he is harsh? What if he drinks? What if he is unfaithful? What if he beats you? Let me be clear about several things. First, in First Peter chapter three, God speaks directly to wives with unbelieving husbands. He says they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives. Your prayers, your kindness, your patience, your godly character — these are powerful. Do not stop praying. Do not stop showing Christ. Second, respecting your husband does not mean allowing him to destroy you or your children. If there is physical danger, please seek the help of your pastor, your church, trusted family members, or proper authorities. God does not require you to stay in a situation that endangers your life. Third, do not suffer in silence if you need help. Find an older Christian woman in your church who can walk with you and pray with you. You are not alone.

Let me close with a woman from church history. Katherine von Bora was a nun who left her convent and married the great Reformer Martin Luther. She managed their large household, raised their children, entertained guests, brewed beer to earn income, and supported her husband's massive work of Bible translation and teaching. Luther called her his "morning star" and his "Lord Kate" — a playful nickname that showed his deep respect for her. Their marriage became a model of Christian family life in the Protestant world for centuries to come. You may never translate a Bible, but the way you love and respect your husband may be a testimony that lasts for generations.

A Prayer Dear Lord, I thank You for the gift of marriage, which You designed from the beginning.

If I am married, I pray for my husband today. Bless him, protect him, draw him close to You. Help me to love him with a love that reflects Your love for the Church. Help me to respect him, to build him up, to pray for him faithfully. Give me a meek and quiet spirit that is precious in Your sight. Where our marriage is hard, give us grace to work through it together. Where there is bitterness, bring forgiveness. Where there is distance, bring closeness. Make our home a place where You are honored, and where our children see the beauty of a Christian marriage. In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: Flourishing in Singleness
fields.body_html:
"A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation. God setteth the solitary in families." Psalm 68:5-6 (KJV) In the last chapter we considered the calling of the Christian wife. But we must not turn the page without pausing to speak to those of our sisters who are not married. Not every woman is called to be a wife. Some of you reading this are single and hope to be married one day. Others are in a season of waiting, not knowing what the Lord will do. Others have been widowed and find yourselves alone after many years of marriage. Others have been divorced or abandoned through no fault of your own. And some of you may sense that God is calling you to remain unmarried for the sake of His Kingdom. Whatever your situation, this chapter is for you. You are not a lesser daughter of God because you are not married. You are fully loved, fully called, and fully able to bring great glory to Christ.

Let me speak plainly about the pressures many single women in East Africa face. From a young age, you have been told that a woman's worth is measured by marriage. Aunties ask when you will bring someone home. Women at the market whisper about why you are still alone. Some even suggest that something must be wrong with you, or that perhaps you have been cursed. Family members may try to arrange marriages you do not want. The pressure to marry — even to marry an unbeliever or a man of poor character just to have a husband — can feel suffocating. My sister, hear what the scriptures say. Your identity is not in whether a man has chosen you. Your identity is in the fact that the King of Heaven has chosen you. He loved you before the foundation of the world. He died for you on the cross. He lives in you by His Spirit. No earthly marriage can add to that, and no earthly singleness can take it away.

Consider our Lord Jesus Himself. He walked this earth for thirty-three years, and He never took a wife. He was the most fully alive person who has ever lived. He was the most loving, the most joyful, the most purposeful. His heart was not divided. His life was not less because He was unmarried. It was, in fact, more — because He was free to give Himself entirely to the mission the Father had sent Him to do. If singleness was good enough for our Lord, it is good enough for His daughters.

The apostle Paul, in First Corinthians chapter seven, writes at length about singleness and marriage. He says plainly that the unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. She is able to attend upon the Lord without distraction. Paul is not teaching that marriage is bad — he has already said that marriage is honourable. What he is saying is that singleness is a gift with its own unique opportunities. The unmarried Christian woman has time, energy, and focus that the married woman often does not. She can pray longer.

She can serve more deeply. She can go where a married woman cannot easily go. She can give herself, undivided, to the work of her Lord.

Look at the women of scripture who served God mightily while unmarried. Anna the prophetess, whom we met earlier, was widowed after only seven years of marriage. She could have spent her remaining years in bitterness, wondering what might have been. Instead, she gave herself to the Lord. She spent more than sixty years in the temple, fasting and praying night and day, and she was rewarded by being among the first to recognize the infant Messiah. Her singleness was not wasted. It was the very soil in which her great ministry of prayer grew.

Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, is never said to be married. She is remembered for sitting at the feet of Jesus and drinking in His teaching. She is remembered for anointing Him with precious oil before His death. Her undivided devotion to Christ was so beautiful that Jesus Himself said her act of love would be told wherever the gospel is preached, to the end of the age.

Mary Magdalene, whom Jesus delivered from seven demons, followed Him in His travels, supported His ministry from her own resources, stood at the foot of the cross when most of the men had fled, and was the first to see the risen Lord on Easter morning. Nothing in scripture suggests she was married. Her whole life was given to her Saviour.

Lydia of Philippi ran her own business selling purple cloth. No husband is mentioned. She led her household in baptism after her conversion. She hosted the first church in Europe in her home.

Whether she had been widowed or had never married, she used her freedom, her resources, and her home for the Kingdom of God.

Dorcas of Joppa made clothes for widows. The four virgin daughters of Philip the evangelist prophesied in the power of the Spirit. Miriam led the women of Israel in song after the Red Sea.

Again and again, scripture honors the contribution of women who were not married.

The history of the Church is full of single women whose lives bore extraordinary fruit. Amy Carmichael went from Northern Ireland to India in 1895 and never married. She founded the Dohnavur Fellowship, a refuge for girls who had been forced into temple prostitution. She rescued hundreds of children, wrote more than thirty books, and served in India for fifty-five years without a single furlough home. Mary Slessor of Scotland, whom we have met before, was engaged twice but remained unmarried for the sake of the gospel. She adopted nine orphans, ended the killing of twin babies among the people she served in West Africa, and opened the way for the gospel in regions where no missionary had dared to go. Gladys Aylward walked over the mountains of China leading a hundred orphan children to safety during the Japanese invasion. Helen Roseveare served as a single medical missionary in the Congo, endured great suffering, and planted hospitals and churches that stand to this day. Corrie ten Boom, after hiding Jews from the Nazis and surviving a concentration camp, spent the rest of her life telling the world that there is no pit so deep that God's love is not deeper still. Every one of these women was single. Every one of them changed the world.

Now hear this beautiful truth, and let it settle deep into your heart. No Christian is truly single.

You have been born again into the family of God. The apostle Paul writes in Ephesians that we are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God. Psalm sixty-eight says that God sets the solitary in families. When Jesus was told that His mother and brothers were outside looking for Him, He looked around at His disciples and said that whoever does the will of God is His brother and sister and mother. The Church is your family. Older believers become your mothers and fathers in the faith. Younger believers become your spiritual sons and daughters. Fellow believers of your own age become your brothers and sisters in Christ. You have a family larger and deeper than any biological family could ever be.

This is not just a pretty idea. It is a practical reality that must be lived out in the local church. If you are a single woman, do not hide yourself at home. Come to the fellowship. Let yourself be known. Find an older woman who can mother you. Find younger women you can encourage. Eat in the homes of families, and invite families into your home. Celebrate Christmas and Easter with the saints if you do not have family nearby. Grieve in their arms when grief comes. Rejoice with them in their joys. This is what the body of Christ is for.

Let me speak practically now. If you are single in this season, whether for now or for life, how should you live?

First, prioritize God with an undivided heart. This is your unique season of opportunity. Pray more.

Read more. Fast sometimes. Listen to Him. Let Him be your first and deepest love. A woman whose heart is fully set on the Lord cannot be shaken by the pressures of the world. This is the foundation of everything else.

Second, embrace the church family. Do not isolate. Do not stay home on Sunday because you feel out of place as the only unmarried woman in your row. Do not skip the women's fellowship because it seems full of wives and mothers. Show up. Serve. Love the families in your church. Ask godly older sisters to walk with you. Let the Body of Christ be your family, not just in name but in daily practice.

Third, serve with your whole heart. You have time that married women often do not have. You have energy to give. Consider missions. Consider teaching. Consider starting a ministry to widows, or orphans, or teenage girls, or women in prison. Consider going where others cannot easily go.

The Kingdom of God has always been advanced in large part by single women who had the freedom to give themselves fully. There may be a work God has for you that no one else can do.

Fourth, work hard and pursue excellence. Do not put your life on hold waiting for marriage. Pursue your education. Grow in your career. Start the business. Plant the garden. Buy the land. Learn the skill. Write the book. Save your money wisely. Be the Proverbs 31 woman in the stage of life you are in. Almost every part of that beautiful chapter applies to a single woman as much as to a married one. A hard-working, God-fearing single woman is a powerful testimony in a lazy and complaining generation.

Fifth, guard your heart and your body. Purity matters deeply. Do not give yourself to a man who has not committed himself to you before God and the Church. Do not date unbelievers, no matter how kind or handsome they may seem — you cannot build a Christian home on a foundation that is not Christian. Do not believe the lie that a bad marriage is better than no marriage. It is not. A godly singleness is a thousand times better than an ungodly marriage. Wait for God's best. If He does not bring marriage, then what He brings instead will be equally good, because He is a good Father.

Sixth, cultivate contentment. Contentment is not resignation. It is not giving up on marriage or pretending you do not desire it. It is the deep peace of trusting that God is good and that His plan for your life is good. Paul wrote from a Roman prison that he had learned, in whatever state he was, to be content. That learning is a journey. It comes through prayer, through scripture, through the gentle work of the Holy Spirit. Ask God to teach you this grace.

A word to those who have been widowed. God sees your grief. He is near to the brokenhearted.

Isaiah fifty-four says that your Maker is your husband — the Lord of hosts is His name. He will not leave you. Find your comfort in Him, and find your family in the Church. Many of the most powerful women in scripture and in history have been widows. Your best years of ministry may still be ahead of you.

A word to those who have been divorced or abandoned. You are not damaged goods. The God who restores all things can restore you. Whatever your past, the blood of Jesus makes you clean and new. Do not let shame keep you from the fellowship of believers. Come. Serve. Love. You belong.

My sister, whether married or single, widowed or waiting, you are loved. The Lord has not forgotten you. He is writing your story, and it is a beautiful one, though the full beauty will only be seen in eternity. Trust Him with this season of your life. Do not waste it waiting for another season to begin. Bloom where He has planted you. Serve where He has placed you. Love whom He has put in front of you. The world will know He is real, in part, because of the joy on the face of a single Christian woman who has found her all in Him.

A Prayer Heavenly Father, I thank You that my worth is not in whether I am married, but in the fact that I am Yours. Thank You for making me Your daughter and for placing me in Your great family, the Church. If I am single in this season, help me to use this time for Your glory.

Give me an undivided heart. Make me a woman of prayer, of service, and of purpose.

Protect me from loneliness and from settling for less than Your best. Surround me with brothers and sisters who love me as Your family. If You call me to marriage one day, prepare me and prepare him. If You call me to singleness for a lifetime, make me fruitful in ways I cannot imagine. Help me to love and support others in every season, just as You have loved me. In the precious name of Jesus, Amen.

And some of you may sense that God is calling you to remain unmarried for the sake of His Kingdom. Whatever your situation, this chapter is for you. You are not a lesser daughter of God because you are not married. You are fully loved, fully called, and fully able to bring great glory to Christ. Let me speak plainly about the pressures many single women in East Africa face. From a young age, you have been told that a woman's worth is measured by marriage. Aunties ask when you will bring someone home. Women at the market whisper about why you are still alone. Some even suggest that something must be wrong with you, or that perhaps you have been cursed. Family members may try to arrange marriages you do not want. The pressure to marry — even to marry an unbeliever or a man of poor character just to have a husband — can feel suffocating. My sister, hear what the scriptures say. Your identity is not in whether a man has chosen you. Your identity is in the fact that the King of Heaven has chosen you. He loved you before the foundation of the world. He died for you on the cross. He lives in you by His Spirit. No earthly marriage can add to that, and no earthly singleness can take it away. Consider our Lord Jesus Himself. He walked this earth for thirty-three years, and He never took a wife. He was the most fully alive person who has ever lived. He was the most loving, the most joyful, the most purposeful. His heart was not divided. His life was not less because He was unmarried. It was, in fact, more — because He was free to give Himself entirely to the mission the Father had sent Him to do. If singleness was good enough for our Lord, it is good enough for His daughters. The apostle Paul, in First Corinthians chapter seven, writes at length about singleness and marriage. He says plainly that the unmarried woman cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit. She is able to attend upon the Lord without distraction. Paul is not teaching that marriage is bad — he has already said that marriage is honourable. What he is saying is that singleness is a gift with its own unique opportunities. The unmarried Christian woman has time, energy, and focus that the married woman often does not. She can pray longer. She can serve more deeply. She can go where a married woman cannot easily go. She can give herself, undivided, to the work of her Lord. Look at the women of scripture who served God mightily while unmarried. Anna the prophetess, whom we met earlier, was widowed after only seven years of marriage. She could have spent her remaining years in bitterness, wondering what might have been. Instead, she gave herself to the Lord. She spent more than sixty years in the temple, fasting and praying night and day, and she was rewarded by being among the first to recognize the infant Messiah. Her singleness was not wasted. It was the very soil in which her great ministry of prayer grew. Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, is never said to be married. She is remembered for sitting at the feet of Jesus and drinking in His teaching. She is remembered for anointing Him with precious oil before His death. Her undivided devotion to Christ was so beautiful that Jesus Himself said her act of love would be told wherever the gospel is preached, to the end of the age. Mary Magdalene, whom Jesus delivered from seven demons, followed Him in His travels, supported His ministry from her own resources, stood at the foot of the cross when most of the men had fled, and was the first to see the risen Lord on Easter morning. Nothing in scripture suggests she was married. Her whole life was given to her Saviour. Lydia of Philippi ran her own business selling purple cloth. No husband is mentioned. She led her household in baptism after her conversion. She hosted the first church in Europe in her home. Whether she had been widowed or had never married, she used her freedom, her resources, and her home for the Kingdom of God. Dorcas of Joppa made clothes for widows. The four virgin daughters of Philip the evangelist prophesied in the power of the Spirit. Miriam led the women of Israel in song after the Red Sea. Again and again, scripture honors the contribution of women who were not married. The history of the Church is full of single women whose lives bore extraordinary fruit. Amy Carmichael went from Northern Ireland to India in 1895 and never married. She founded the Dohnavur Fellowship, a refuge for girls who had been forced into temple prostitution. She rescued hundreds of children, wrote more than thirty books, and served in India for fifty-five years without a single furlough home. Mary Slessor of Scotland, whom we have met before, was engaged twice but remained unmarried for the sake of the gospel. She adopted nine orphans, ended the killing of twin babies among the people she served in West Africa, and opened the way for the gospel in regions where no missionary had dared to go. Gladys Aylward walked over the mountains of China leading a hundred orphan children to safety during the Japanese invasion. Helen Roseveare served as a single medical missionary in the Congo, endured great suffering, and planted hospitals and churches that stand to this day. Corrie ten Boom, after hiding Jews from the Nazis and surviving a concentration camp, spent the rest of her life telling the world that there is no pit so deep that God's love is not deeper still. Every one of these women was single. Every one of them changed the world. Now hear this beautiful truth, and let it settle deep into your heart. No Christian is truly single. You have been born again into the family of God. The apostle Paul writes in Ephesians that we are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God. Psalm sixty-eight says that God sets the solitary in families. When Jesus was told that His mother and brothers were outside looking for Him, He looked around at His disciples and said that whoever does the will of God is His brother and sister and mother. The Church is your family. Older believers become your mothers and fathers in the faith. Younger believers become your spiritual sons and daughters. Fellow believers of your own age become your brothers and sisters in Christ. You have a family larger and deeper than any biological family could ever be. This is not just a pretty idea. It is a practical reality that must be lived out in the local church. If you are a single woman, do not hide yourself at home. Come to the fellowship. Let yourself be known. Find an older woman who can mother you. Find younger women you can encourage. Eat in the homes of families, and invite families into your home. Celebrate Christmas and Easter with the saints if you do not have family nearby. Grieve in their arms when grief comes. Rejoice with them in their joys. This is what the body of Christ is for. Let me speak practically now. If you are single in this season, whether for now or for life, how should you live? First, prioritize God with an undivided heart. This is your unique season of opportunity. Pray more. Read more. Fast sometimes. Listen to Him. Let Him be your first and deepest love. A woman whose heart is fully set on the Lord cannot be shaken by the pressures of the world. This is the foundation of everything else. Second, embrace the church family. Do not isolate. Do not stay home on Sunday because you feel out of place as the only unmarried woman in your row. Do not skip the women's fellowship because it seems full of wives and mothers. Show up. Serve. Love the families in your church. Ask godly older sisters to walk with you. Let the Body of Christ be your family, not just in name but in daily practice. Third, serve with your whole heart. You have time that married women often do not have. You have energy to give. Consider missions. Consider teaching. Consider starting a ministry to widows, or orphans, or teenage girls, or women in prison. Consider going where others cannot easily go. The Kingdom of God has always been advanced in large part by single women who had the freedom to give themselves fully. There may be a work God has for you that no one else can do. Fourth, work hard and pursue excellence. Do not put your life on hold waiting for marriage. Pursue your education. Grow in your career. Start the business. Plant the garden. Buy the land. Learn the skill. Write the book. Save your money wisely. Be the Proverbs 31 woman in the stage of life you are in. Almost every part of that beautiful chapter applies to a single woman as much as to a married one. A hard-working, God-fearing single woman is a powerful testimony in a lazy and complaining generation. Fifth, guard your heart and your body. Purity matters deeply. Do not give yourself to a man who has not committed himself to you before God and the Church. Do not date unbelievers, no matter how kind or handsome they may seem — you cannot build a Christian home on a foundation that is not Christian. Do not believe the lie that a bad marriage is better than no marriage. It is not. A godly singleness is a thousand times better than an ungodly marriage. Wait for God's best. If He does not bring marriage, then what He brings instead will be equally good, because He is a good Father. Sixth, cultivate contentment. Contentment is not resignation. It is not giving up on marriage or pretending you do not desire it. It is the deep peace of trusting that God is good and that His plan for your life is good. Paul wrote from a Roman prison that he had learned, in whatever state he was, to be content. That learning is a journey. It comes through prayer, through scripture, through the gentle work of the Holy Spirit. Ask God to teach you this grace. A word to those who have been widowed. God sees your grief. He is near to the brokenhearted. Isaiah fifty-four says that your Maker is your husband — the Lord of hosts is His name. He will not leave you. Find your comfort in Him, and find your family in the Church. Many of the most powerful women in scripture and in history have been widows. Your best years of ministry may still be ahead of you. A word to those who have been divorced or abandoned. You are not damaged goods. The God who restores all things can restore you. Whatever your past, the blood of Jesus makes you clean and new. Do not let shame keep you from the fellowship of believers. Come. Serve. Love. You belong. My sister, whether married or single, widowed or waiting, you are loved. The Lord has not forgotten you. He is writing your story, and it is a beautiful one, though the full beauty will only be seen in eternity. Trust Him with this season of your life. Do not waste it waiting for another season to begin. Bloom where He has planted you. Serve where He has placed you. Love whom He has put in front of you. The world will know He is real, in part, because of the joy on the face of a single Christian woman who has found her all in Him. A Prayer Heavenly Father, I thank You that my worth is not in whether I am married, but in the fact that I am Yours. Thank You for making me Your daughter and for placing me in Your great family, the Church. If I am single in this season, help me to use this time for Your glory. Give me an undivided heart. Make me a woman of prayer, of service, and of purpose. Protect me from loneliness and from settling for less than Your best. Surround me with brothers and sisters who love me as Your family. If You call me to marriage one day, prepare me and prepare him. If You call me to singleness for a lifetime, make me fruitful in ways I cannot imagine. Help me to love and support others in every season, just as You have loved me. In the precious name of Jesus, Amen.

fields.title: Nurturing the Next Generation: Raising Godly Children
fields.body_html:
"And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Deuteronomy 6:6-7 (KJV) There is no greater mission field on earth than your own home. The children God has placed in your care are the next generation of the Church, the next leaders of your village, your town, your nation. How they are raised will determine whether the gospel advances or retreats in East Africa in the years to come. And under God, no one has more influence on a child in the early years than the mother.

In the Old Testament, God gave clear instructions to parents. The Shema, in Deuteronomy chapter six, tells parents to teach the commandments of God to their children diligently. The word "diligently" is important. It is not casual teaching, not something done only on Sunday mornings, but constant, ongoing, woven into every moment of life. As you walk, as you sit, as you lie down, as you rise up — the truth of God is to be spoken, modeled, and repeated.

Consider Jochebed, the mother of Moses. She lived under Pharaoh's terrible decree that all Hebrew baby boys must be thrown into the Nile. But she feared God more than she feared Pharaoh. She hid her baby for three months. Then, when she could no longer hide him, she made a small basket of reeds, covered it with tar, placed her son inside, and set him among the reeds of the river. Her daughter Miriam watched nearby. When Pharaoh's daughter found the baby, Miriam stepped forward and offered to find a Hebrew woman to nurse him. In God's providence, Jochebed was hired to nurse her own son. For the first years of his life — perhaps three or four years, which in that time was how long children nursed — Moses grew up in his mother's arms, hearing of the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. She had only a few short years to pour into him before he was handed over to Pharaoh's palace. But those years were enough. The identity of Moses was set.

He knew who he was. He knew whose he was. And many decades later, he chose to suffer with the people of God rather than enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season. Mothers, never underestimate the value of those early years. Whatever you plant in the first five years of a child's life will bear fruit for a lifetime.

Consider Hannah again. When she received her son Samuel, she did not cling to him. She weaned him, and then brought him to the tabernacle and gave him to serve the Lord all the days of his life.

Each year she would come and bring him a little coat she had made. Imagine that. Every year she sewed a coat and delivered it to her son, who was serving in the house of God. Samuel grew up in the presence of the Lord. His mother had dedicated him before he was born, and she continued to invest in him even after he left her home. Dedicate your children to God, sister. Not just at a baby dedication ceremony, but every day. Lay them on the altar of the Lord in prayer. Trust God to use them for His glory.

Consider Eunice and Lois, the mother and grandmother of Timothy. Paul writes that the unfeigned faith that was in Timothy dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and in his mother Eunice. Three generations of faith in one family. And yet Timothy's father was a Greek, probably not a believer.

Sometimes a godly mother and grandmother must carry the spiritual weight of the family. They carried it faithfully. And Timothy became a pastor and a close companion of Paul. My sister, whether or not your husband is a strong spiritual leader, you can be a Eunice and a Lois. You can raise children who know the scriptures from their earliest days.

Now let me speak practically. How do you raise godly children in the East Africa of today, when so many influences pull against you — poverty, peer pressure, immoral entertainment, schools that do not teach Christian values, even unbelieving relatives?

First, establish family worship. Every day, if possible. Gather the family, even if only for ten or fifteen minutes. Read a short passage of scripture. Explain it in simple words. Pray. Sing a song of praise. If your children are young, keep it short. As they grow older, make it richer. Do not skip this even when you are tired. Even when the house is busy. The consistency of family worship will shape your children more than any sermon they hear on Sunday.

Second, teach them to pray. Teach them simple prayers at first. Thank God for the food. Thank God for the day. Pray for Baba when he is away at work. Pray for the sick auntie.

As they grow, teach them to pray. Teach them to pray for themselves, their friends, their teachers, their nation. A child who learns to pray young will be a praying adult.

Third, teach them to obey. The Bible commands children to honor and obey their parents. This is the first commandment with a promise. A child who does not learn to obey a parent will struggle later to obey a boss, a pastor, or the Lord Himself. Do not be afraid to discipline. The book of Proverbs says that he who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him promptly. Discipline, however, must never be done in anger or in cruelty. It must be done in love, with explanation, followed by forgiveness and affection. Your children should never doubt that you love them, even when you must correct them.

Fourth, teach them the difference between right and wrong in everyday life. Teach them to be truthful. Teach them to work hard at their studies. Teach them to be kind to their siblings. Teach them to be helpful around the home — boys as well as girls should be taught to fetch water, to sweep, to help with cooking. Teach them to respect their elders. Teach them to be modest in their dress and speech. Teach them to keep away from bad company, for evil companions corrupt good character.

Fifth, tell them stories. African mothers have always been great storytellers. Tell them the stories of the Bible — Noah and the flood, David and Goliath, Daniel and the lions, the good Samaritan, the prodigal son. Tell them the stories of the Uganda Martyrs, of young Kizito and Mbaga and Gyaviira, who died rather than deny their faith. Tell them of Mary Slessor, the small Scottish woman who went to West Africa and saved the lives of twin babies who had been left to die. Tell them of Simeon Nsibambi, who prayed for revival in Uganda. Stories put truth into the heart in a way that lectures never can.

Sixth, be present. Children do not care for expensive gifts nearly as much as they care for your time, your attention, your affection. Sit with them. Listen to them. Learn their names, their friends, their fears, their dreams. Know what is happening in their school, in their heart, in their life.

Children who feel known and loved at home are far less likely to run to the world looking for love elsewhere.

Seventh, model what you teach. Children learn more from what you do than from what you say.

If you tell them not to lie but they hear you lie to the neighbor, they will learn to lie. If you tell them to forgive but they see you holding grudges, they will hold grudges. If you tell them to pray but they never see you pray, they will not pray. But if you live what you teach, it will be written on their hearts.

Do not be discouraged if your children do not immediately show the fruit of your teaching. Some children receive the faith quickly. Others go through a wandering season before they return.

Remember Augustine and Monica. Thirty years of tears and prayer preceded his conversion. Keep sowing. Keep praying. The God who began a good work in your family will be faithful to complete it.

One more thing. Some of you reading this may not have biological children. Perhaps God has not given you children yet. Perhaps He has chosen another path for your life. Do not feel that this chapter does not apply to you. God may give you nieces and nephews to pour into. He may give you spiritual daughters in the faith. He may give you a ministry to orphans — and God knows East Africa has many orphans who need Christian aunties. The maternal heart God has placed in you can nurture many children, whether they came from your own body or not.

A Prayer Father, I bring to You the children in my life. I thank You for them. Help me to see them as You see them — as eternal souls whom You have entrusted to my care. Give me the strength to teach them Your ways with diligence. Give me wisdom when I must correct them. Give me patience when I am weary. Cover them with Your mercy when I fail. Save them, Lord.

Call them into Your kingdom. Use them for Your purposes. Let my home be a place where You are known and loved, and where the next generation learns to walk with You. In the name of Jesus, Amen.

fields.title: Managing Your Household with Wisdom
fields.body_html:
"She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." Proverbs 31:27 (KJV) Proverbs chapter thirty-one paints a picture of a remarkable woman. She has become known as the virtuous woman or the Proverbs 31 woman. Her husband trusts in her. Her children rise up and call her blessed. She works with willing hands. She rises while it is yet night to prepare food for her family. She considers a field and buys it. She plants a vineyard. She makes clothing and sells it to the merchants. She reaches out her hands to the poor and needy. She is clothed with strength and dignity, and she laughs at the days to come. This is not a weak woman. This is a strong, wise, hard-working, godly woman. And at the heart of her life is her household.

Managing a household is not a small calling. It is not less important than running a business or holding a job in an office. In many ways, it is more important, because the household is where the next generation is shaped. A peaceful, well-ordered home is a powerful testimony to the gospel. A chaotic, quarrelsome home drives everyone in it — husband, children, and guests — toward the door.

The Bible says that a wise woman builds her house, but a foolish woman tears it down with her own hands. What does it mean to build your house? Let me walk through several areas.

First, there is the physical ordering of the home. Your house does not need to be large or beautiful to be a good home. You can make a mud-brick house with an iron-sheet roof a peaceful sanctuary for your family. What matters is cleanliness, orderliness, and care. Keep the floors swept. Keep the dishes washed. Keep the clothes laundered. Keep the compound free of trash. Teach your children to help with these things from an early age. It is not shameful for a woman to be skilled in these household arts. It is a beautiful thing. The Shunammite woman in Second Kings chapter four is a wonderful example. She noticed that the prophet Elisha was passing through her town often, and she said to her husband, "Let us make a small chamber on the wall, and put there for him a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick." She planned. She arranged. She used what she had to bless a man of God. Her household was orderly enough that she could offer hospitality at any time.

Second, there is the feeding of the household. The Proverbs 31 woman brings her food from afar.

She rises early and gives meat to her household. Feeding a family well, on a tight budget, is one of the great skills of the Christian wife. Learn to cook well the foods of your people — matoke, beans, rice, ugali, sukuma wiki, groundnut stew, chapati. Learn to preserve food — drying, smoking, pickling — so that nothing is wasted. Teach your daughters to cook. Do not allow them to grow up unable to care for a family. Meals are not only about food. They are about family life.

The dinner table is where the day is shared, where teaching happens, where prayer is made, where bonds are strengthened. Make mealtimes special, even when the food is simple.

Third, there is the management of money. This is one of the hardest areas for many families.

Money comes in unpredictably. Needs are many. Pressures come from extended family.

Temptations abound. But the wise Christian woman learns to handle money with care, according to biblical principles. Give to the Lord first — the Bible teaches us to honor the Lord with the firstfruits of all our increase. Save something, even a little. The Proverbs 31 woman bought a field from her own earnings, which means she was able to save and invest. Avoid debt, especially to those who charge high interest. Live within your means. Plan for expenses that you know are coming — school fees, medical costs, funerals. Do not spend money on foolish things while necessary things go unmet. Work alongside your husband on these matters. Do not hide spending from him. Pray together over financial decisions.

Fourth, there is the making of a home atmosphere. This is harder to measure but perhaps more important than anything else. What is the feeling in your home? Is it peaceful or tense? Is it joyful or heavy? Is it a place people want to come to or a place people want to escape from? The spirit of a home is shaped largely by the woman in it. If the wife and mother is anxious, the whole family will be anxious. If she is contentious, the whole family will argue. If she is trusting God and walking in joy, the whole family will feel the peace. You may not be able to control what happens outside your gate, but by the grace of God, you can set the tone inside your gate. Play good gospel music. fields.title: Teaching Women and Children
fields.body_html:
"The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things; that they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children." Titus 2:3-4 (KJV) One of the most overlooked ministries in the Church today is the teaching ministry of older Christian women to younger Christian women. Paul told Titus, a young pastor, that this was to be a standard practice in the church. The older women were to teach the younger women how to love their husbands, how to love their children, how to be sober and discreet and chaste, how to keep their homes, how to be good. This is not optional. It is part of God's design for how the faith is passed from one generation to the next.

Why does God command older women to teach younger women? Because some things are better taught woman to woman. A young wife may not feel comfortable asking her pastor about struggles in her marriage. A new mother may need practical advice from someone who has walked the road before her. A young Christian may need an older woman to pray with her through a hard decision.

These mentoring relationships are precious and powerful.

If you are an older woman reading this — by which I mean any woman who has walked with Christ longer than someone younger — you have something to give. You do not need to be a Bible school graduate. You do not need to be a pastor's wife. You do not need to have all the answers.

You only need to have walked with the Lord, to know your Bible, and to be willing to pour into the next generation.

If you are a younger woman, seek out an older sister in the Lord. Ask her to meet with you, perhaps once a month or once a week. Ask her your questions. Learn from her life. Pray with her. The Bible tells us that in a multitude of counselors there is safety. Do not try to walk the Christian life alone.

The Bible gives us many examples of women teaching women and children. Consider Deborah in the book of Judges. She was a prophetess who judged Israel in a time of great darkness. She sat under a palm tree, and the people came up to her for judgment. She also led the nation into battle with the warrior Barak, because Barak would not go unless she went with him. Deborah was a mother in Israel — that was how she described herself in her song of victory. She taught the people the ways of the Lord, and she showed courage in battle. God uses women as teachers and leaders in His people.

Consider Priscilla again. When she and her husband Aquila heard Apollos teaching in the synagogue — Apollos was an eloquent man who knew the scriptures but had not yet heard the full message of Jesus and the baptism of the Holy Spirit — they took him aside and expounded to him the way of God more perfectly. Priscilla taught Apollos. She did so quietly, alongside her husband, not in a public setting, but her knowledge of the scriptures was deep enough to teach a gifted preacher. Many young men have been helped along their way by a godly woman who took the time to explain something they did not yet understand.

Consider Naomi and Ruth. When Ruth returned with Naomi to Bethlehem, she followed Naomi's instructions carefully. Naomi taught her about the ways of the Israelites. Naomi taught her how to approach Boaz in the matter of kinsman redemption. Ruth obeyed Naomi, and the result was her marriage to Boaz and her place in the genealogy of King David and of Jesus Christ. A young woman who listens to the wise counsel of an older godly woman is set on a path of blessing.

In the history of the East African Revival, women were central to the spread of the gospel. Women like Blasio Kigozi's wife, and many others whose names are not recorded in books but are written in heaven, gathered other women for fellowship, Bible study, and prayer. They went from village to village, house to house, telling other women about Jesus and about the walking in the light.

Their simple, faithful testimony reshaped the Church in East Africa.

Think also of Mary Slessor, who went as a missionary from Scotland to Calabar in present-day Nigeria in the 1800s. She learned the language of the people. She lived among them. She taught the women that twin babies should not be killed as had been the custom. She taught them about Jesus. She raised abandoned children as her own. Her impact on the region was so great that she is still remembered today. One small, determined Scottish woman changed the lives of thousands of African women and children.

Or consider Mama Mary Stuart, who came from Ireland to Uganda in the early 1900s and founded Gayaza High School in 1905. She believed that African girls deserved a Christian education as much as African boys. She built a school where girls could learn the scriptures, develop their minds, and prepare for godly womanhood. A century later, Gayaza is still a leading school, and its alumni are found in every sphere of Ugandan life.

You do not have to cross an ocean to be a teacher of women and children. You can do it in your church, in your neighborhood, in your family. Let me suggest some practical ways.

Start with children. Volunteer in the Sunday School. The stories you tell, the verses you teach, the love you show will shape little ones for a lifetime. Do not think that teaching children is less important than teaching adults. Jesus said that of such is the kingdom of heaven.

Start a small women's fellowship. It does not need to be big. Gather three or four women in your home. Read a chapter of the Bible. Discuss it. Pray together. Share your joys and your burdens.

Over time, invite others to join. Some of the strongest women's ministries in the world began with two or three women meeting in a small room.

Disciple one younger woman. Look around your church. Who is a new believer, or a young wife, or a new mother, who could benefit from a godly older sister? Ask the Lord whom you should invest in. Then invite her for tea. Ask her questions. Share what you have learned. Walk with her for a season.

Teach with your life first. Paul told Titus that the older women must be in behavior as becometh holiness. You cannot teach what you are not. If you are to teach younger women to love their husbands, you must love yours. If you are to teach them to manage their children, you must manage yours. This is not about being perfect. It is about walking the walk, repenting when you fall, and being genuine.

Use what God has put in your hand. Maybe you have a gift for hospitality — teach the young women to welcome others. Maybe you have a gift for prayer — teach them to intercede. Maybe you have a gift for the scriptures — teach them the Word. Maybe you have a gift for encouragement — teach them to build up rather than tear down. God has given each one of us something. Do not bury your talent. Invest it.

A Prayer Father, raise up in our churches women who teach women, and older women who pour into younger women. Help me to receive gladly from those who are further along, and to give willingly to those coming after me. Give me wisdom, humility, and love. Let the faith passed down from Lois to Eunice to Timothy be passed down in our generation as well.

Make me a mother in Israel, whatever my age, for the sake of Your Kingdom. In the name of Jesus, Amen.
