fields.title: Guarding Your Heart: Emotions, Tongue, and Gentle Spirit
fields.body_html:
"But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price." 1 Peter 3:4 (KJV) The book of Proverbs warns us to guard our hearts with all diligence, for out of the heart flow the issues of life. Everything that comes out of your mouth — every word you speak to your husband, every correction you give your child, every greeting you offer the neighbor, every complaint you make — flows first from your heart. If your heart is full of peace, peace will come out. If your heart is full of anger, anger will come out. If your heart is full of bitterness, bitter words will come out. That is why the Lord Jesus said that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.

The Christian woman has been given, by the grace of God, a new heart. When you came to Christ, He took out the heart of stone and gave you a heart of flesh. He put His Spirit within you. But even so, you must still learn daily to walk in the Spirit and not in the flesh. Old habits of anger, jealousy, fear, self-pity, and bitterness do not disappear overnight. They must be put to death one day at a time.

Let me speak about several emotions that can trouble a Christian woman, and how the scriptures help us handle them.

First, anger. There is an anger that is right — the Lord Jesus was angry at the moneychangers in the temple. But most of our anger is not righteous. It is fleshly. It comes because our pride is wounded, because we did not get our way, because someone crossed us, because we are tired. The Bible says, be angry and sin not, and let not the sun go down on your wrath. That means, deal with your anger quickly. Go to God. Confess it. Ask for His help. If you have wronged someone in your anger, go and make peace. Do not let anger simmer in your heart. If it does, it will turn to bitterness, and bitterness is a poison that kills marriages, families, and friendships.

Second, fear. Every woman has fears. Fear for her children's safety. Fear for her health. Fear of poverty. Fear of what people will say. Fear of the future. The Bible tells us again and again, fear not, for I am with thee. Isaiah 41:10 is a precious verse to memorize: "Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness." When fear comes, speak the word of God to your own soul. Pray. Trust. Cast your cares on the Lord, for He cares for you.

Third, jealousy. This is a subtle and dangerous sin. It is the sin of Cain, who killed Abel because God accepted Abel's offering and not his. It is the sin of Miriam, who was struck with leprosy when she envied Moses. It is the sin of Joseph's brothers, who sold him into slavery. Jealousy comes when we compare ourselves to others. She has a better house. She has a better husband. Her children behave better than mine. She has more money. She is prettier. She is more respected at church. When these thoughts come, repent of them quickly. Rejoice with those who rejoice. Thank God for what He has given you. Do not compare yourself. God has a different path for each of His daughters.

Fourth, bitterness. The writer of Hebrews warns us to look diligently lest any root of bitterness spring up and trouble us. Bitterness usually comes from a wound — a deep hurt that has not healed.

Perhaps a husband has disappointed you. Perhaps a family member has cheated you. Perhaps a pastor has hurt you. Perhaps a friend has betrayed you. If you do not deal with the wound through prayer, forgiveness, and often through counsel from wise Christians, the wound becomes a root.

And that root grows until it poisons everything in your life. You must forgive. Forgiveness does not mean what the other person did was right. It does not always mean you will be friends again with that person, especially if they continue to hurt you. Forgiveness means you release them to God and refuse to let their sin control your heart any longer.

Fifth, self-pity. This is a very common sin among women, and it is very subtle. It whispers, "No one understands me. No one cares about me. I am working so hard and no one appreciates it." Self-pity focuses all your attention on yourself. It feeds on private complaining. It leads to depression and resentment. The cure is worship and service. Lift your eyes to the Lord. Count your blessings.

And then go and serve someone else. When you pour out your life for others, the Lord fills your own cup.

Now let us speak of the tongue. The book of James says that the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity.

It can bless, and it can curse. It can build up, and it can tear down. It can speak truth, and it can spread lies. Of all the areas a Christian woman must bring under the Lord's authority, the tongue may be the most important.

The Proverbs warn again and again about the contentious woman. It says it is better to dwell in the corner of a housetop than with a contentious woman in a wide house. It says it is better to dwell in the wilderness than with a contentious and angry woman. The Bible is not harsh on women — it gives the same warnings to men in other forms — but it is honest. A wife whose tongue is sharp can drive her husband away. She can make her children afraid of her. She can fill her home with tension.

On the other hand, consider the Proverbs 31 woman. She opens her mouth with wisdom, and in her tongue is the law of kindness. What a beautiful description. Her words are wise. Her words are kind. She does not speak to wound. She does not speak carelessly. She does not gossip. She does not tear down others. When she speaks, wisdom flows.

Let me speak very practically. Guard your tongue in the marketplace, where women gather. Do not participate in gossip about other women, other families, other churches. If others begin to gossip, find a reason to leave, or gently change the subject. Guard your tongue at home. Do not speak sharply to your husband. Do not nag. Do not answer your children with anger. Guard your tongue in the church. Do not criticize the pastor to others. Do not spread rumors about other members. Guard your tongue on your phone and online. Many Christian women have destroyed their witness by what they write in WhatsApp groups or on Facebook.

Consider the example of Mary, the mother of our Lord. When she received the terrifying news from the angel that she would bear the Son of God as an unmarried virgin, what did she do? She did not argue. She did not run to the neighbors. She said, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." And later, when great things happened around the Christ child — the shepherds came, the wise men came, strange prophecies were spoken — the Bible says she kept all these things and pondered them in her heart. She was a woman of a quiet spirit. She did not need to say everything she thought. She held truth deep in her heart and brought it to God in prayer. That is the kind of spirit the Lord delights in.

Now, a meek and quiet spirit does not mean a woman who never speaks. It does not mean a woman who agrees with sin or who lets herself be walked on. Abigail spoke up boldly to David and saved her household. Esther spoke up boldly to the king and saved her people. The daughters of Zelophehad spoke up boldly to Moses and received their inheritance. The meek and quiet spirit is a spirit that is under the control of the Holy Spirit. It does not speak rashly. It does not speak from anger. When it does speak, it speaks with grace and truth together.

A Prayer Holy Spirit, come and search my heart today. Show me the anger, the fear, the jealousy, the bitterness, the self-pity that I have allowed to take root. I confess these sins to You.

Wash me clean by the blood of Jesus. Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. Give me the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, precious in Your sight. Let my words bring life and not death. Let my heart be a place where Your peace dwells. In Jesus' name, Amen.

It comes because our pride is wounded, because we did not get our way, because someone crossed us, because we are tired. The Bible says, be angry and sin not, and let not the sun go down on your wrath. That means, deal with your anger quickly. Go to God. Confess it. Ask for His help. If you have wronged someone in your anger, go and make peace. Do not let anger simmer in your heart. If it does, it will turn to bitterness, and bitterness is a poison that kills marriages, families, and friendships. Second, fear. Every woman has fears. Fear for her children's safety. Fear for her health. Fear of poverty. Fear of what people will say. Fear of the future. The Bible tells us again and again, fear not, for I am with thee. Isaiah 41:10 is a precious verse to memorize: "Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness." When fear comes, speak the word of God to your own soul. Pray. Trust. Cast your cares on the Lord, for He cares for you. Third, jealousy. This is a subtle and dangerous sin. Thank God for what He has given you. Do not compare yourself. God has a different path for each of His daughters. Fourth, bitterness. Forgiveness means you release them to God and refuse to let their sin control your heart any longer. Fifth, self-pity. This is a very common sin among women, and it is very subtle. It whispers, "No one understands me. No one cares about me. I am working so hard and no one appreciates it." Self-pity focuses all your attention on yourself. It feeds on private complaining. It leads to depression and resentment. The cure is worship and service. Lift your eyes to the Lord. Count your blessings. And then go and serve someone else. She can make her children afraid of her. She can fill her home with tension. On the other hand, consider the Proverbs 31 woman. She opens her mouth with wisdom, and in her tongue is the law of kindness. What a beautiful description. Her words are wise. Her words are kind. She does not speak to wound. She does not speak carelessly. She does not gossip. She does not tear down others. When she speaks, wisdom flows. Let me speak very practically. Guard your tongue in the church. Do not criticize the pastor to others. Do not spread rumors about other members. Guard your tongue on your phone and online. When she received the terrifying news from the angel that she would bear the Son of God as an unmarried virgin, what did she do? She did not argue. She did not run to the neighbors. She said, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." And later, when great things happened around the Christ child — the shepherds came, the wise men came, strange prophecies were spoken — the Bible says she kept all these things and pondered them in her heart. She was a woman of a quiet spirit. She did not need to say everything she thought. She held truth deep in her heart and brought it to God in prayer. That is the kind of spirit the Lord delights in. Now, a meek and quiet spirit does not mean a woman who never speaks. It does not mean a woman who agrees with sin or who lets herself be walked on. Abigail spoke up boldly to David and saved her household. Esther spoke up boldly to the king and saved her people. The daughters of Zelophehad spoke up boldly to Moses and received their inheritance. The meek and quiet spirit is a spirit that is under the control of the Holy Spirit. It does not speak rashly. It does not speak from anger. When it does speak, it speaks with grace and truth together. A Prayer Holy Spirit, come and search my heart today. Show me the anger, the fear, the jealousy, the bitterness, the self-pity that I have allowed to take root. I confess these sins to You. Wash me clean by the blood of Jesus. Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips. Give me the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, precious in Your sight. Let my words bring life and not death. Let my heart be a place where Your peace dwells. In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: Hard Work, Godly Goals, and the Industrious Life
fields.body_html:
"She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms." Proverbs 31:17 (KJV) Some people imagine that the Christian woman is meant to be passive, soft, and dependent. The Bible paints a very different picture. From Genesis to Revelation, the women of God are strong, industrious, and faithful in their work. The Proverbs 31 woman girdeth her loins with strength. She rises while it is yet night. She considers a field and buys it. She perceives that her merchandise is good. Her candle does not go out by night. She is clothed with strength and dignity.

God has given you abilities. He has given you strength in your body, understanding in your mind, creativity in your heart, and skill in your hands. He expects you to use them. In the parable of the talents, the Lord gave to each servant something according to his ability. He expected each one to invest it and to produce a return. The servant who hid his talent was called wicked and lazy. God is not pleased when His daughters bury their gifts in the ground.

Let me speak about four kinds of work — physical work, home economics, income-producing work, and Kingdom work. Each one is part of the calling of the Christian woman.

First, physical work. In many African cultures, women do much of the hardest physical labor. We fetch water, we work the gardens, we carry heavy loads, we cook over fires, we wash clothes by hand. Do not see this work as beneath you. In God's eyes, every honest work is dignified. Jesus Himself worked as a carpenter. His mother Mary surely carried water and ground grain like every woman of her time. Paul, the great apostle, made tents with his own hands. Do your work heartily, as unto the Lord, and not unto men. Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with your might.

Second, home economics. This is the work of managing the resources of the home to meet the needs of the family. The Proverbs 31 woman was skilled in this. She sought wool and flax. She bought food wisely. She made clothing.

She considered what the family would need in the coming months and prepared ahead of time. In our time, home economics includes budgeting, shopping carefully, cooking meals that are nourishing but affordable, preserving food, mending clothes rather than always buying new, and teaching the children how to help. A woman who is skilled in home economics can stretch a small income into a family that is well fed, well clothed, and secure.

Third, income-producing work. The Proverbs 31 woman was not only a keeper of the home. She was also a businesswoman. She considered a field and bought it. With the fruit of her hands she planted a vineyard. She made fine linen and sold it. She delivered girdles to the merchants. Her husband trusted her with the family resources, and she multiplied them. This is a beautiful picture.

It teaches us that a Christian woman can, and in many cases should, contribute to the family's income through her own industry. Many women in East Africa are the economic backbone of their families. You sell in the market. You run a small salon. You keep chickens and sell eggs. You grow beans and matoke for sale. You sew clothes. You make crafts. You teach school. You work as a nurse or a government employee. All of this is good and God-honoring work, when done with integrity and when it does not crowd out your family and your walk with the Lord.

Let me speak about setting godly goals. Goals are important. A ship without a rudder drifts wherever the current takes it. A life without goals drifts as well. The Bible says that where there is no vision, the people perish. As a Christian woman, you should have goals for your spiritual life, your family, your finances, your work, and your service.

Spiritual goals. Perhaps this year you will read through the whole Bible. Perhaps you will memorize fifty-two verses. Perhaps you will start a daily time of prayer and journaling. Perhaps you will read one Christian book about marriage, or prayer, or discipleship.

Family goals. Perhaps this year you will begin family devotions every evening. Perhaps you will have one special meal each week where the whole family sits down together without distractions.

Perhaps you will teach your children one new skill.

Financial goals. Perhaps this year you will save a certain amount each month. Perhaps you will pay off a debt. Perhaps you will start a small side business. Perhaps you will give a larger offering to the Lord than last year.

Work goals. Perhaps this year you will learn a new skill that will help you earn better. Perhaps you will take a short course. Perhaps you will become more organized or more efficient in what you already do.

Service goals. Perhaps this year you will join the women's fellowship. Perhaps you will teach Sunday School. Perhaps you will visit one widow or sick person each week. Perhaps you will disciple a younger woman.

Write your goals down. Pray over them. Review them with your husband if you are married. Share some of them with a godly friend who can hold you accountable. At the end of the year, review what God did.

Let me show you a few women in the scriptures who were industrious and who had goals. Consider Lydia in Acts chapter sixteen. She was a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira. Purple was a luxury product, and her business was probably quite profitable. When she heard Paul preach by the riverside, she received Christ. Her whole household was baptized. She then opened her home to Paul and his team, and the church at Philippi was born in her house. Here was a businesswoman, using her business to support the gospel, and opening her home for the Kingdom.

Consider Dorcas, also called Tabitha, in Acts chapter nine. She lived in Joppa. The scripture says she was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did. When she died, the widows of the city stood weeping and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas had made for them while she was with them. She had taken her skill with needle and thread and used it to clothe the poor. When Peter raised her from the dead, her ministry continued. Your skills — whatever they are — can be used for the glory of God and the good of others.

Consider the woman at the well in John chapter four. Before Jesus met her, she was a broken woman. After she met Jesus, she ran into the city and told everyone about Him. Her bold witness brought many Samaritans to faith. Ministry is not only for pastors. It is for every believer.

One caution as we end this chapter. Work and goals are good, but they are not everything. If your work takes over your life, if your goals push out your walk with God, if your business crowds out your husband and children, then something is out of order. Jesus said that the Father has numbered the hairs of your head. He cares for you. He will provide for you. Do not work seven days a week.

Honor the Sabbath. Rest. Worship. Trust. The Bible says that except the Lord build the house, they labor in vain that build it. You can work hard, but it is God who gives the increase.

Finally, work with honesty and integrity. Do not cheat in the market. Do not give short measure.

Do not lie to customers. Do not pay workers less than what you agreed. Do not take bribes. Do not participate in corruption to get ahead. The God who sees you knows whether your business is conducted in the light or in the darkness. A Christian businesswoman who is known for honesty will, in the long run, be more blessed than one who cuts corners. Integrity is not the easy road. It is the narrow road. But it is the road of blessing.

A Prayer Lord, You are a God who works. From the beginning You labored to create the heavens and the earth. Teach me to work with diligence and skill. Give me strength for my labor.

Give me wisdom to set godly goals and to pursue them. Make my hands useful and my mind clear. Bless the work of my hands that I may provide for my family, give to Your Kingdom, and be a blessing to others. Keep me from laziness, but also keep me from idolizing work.

Let all I do be for Your glory, in the name of Jesus, Amen.

fields.title: Caring for Others: Hospitality and Compassion
fields.body_html:
"Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Hebrews 13:2 (KJV) The heart of the Christian faith is love — love for God and love for neighbor. Jesus said these two commandments sum up the whole law and the prophets. And one of the most beautiful ways the Christian woman expresses this love is through hospitality and compassion toward others. She opens her home. She shares her food. She visits the sick. She cares for the widow and the orphan.

She shows the love of Jesus in practical, tangible ways.

East African culture has always valued hospitality. The stranger at the door is welcomed. Food is shared even when there is little. A visitor is never sent away without at least a cup of tea. This is a beautiful gift of our culture that aligns closely with biblical teaching. But we live in a time when these ancient virtues are under pressure. Life is busier. People live in gated compounds. Fear of strangers is greater. Many women say they have no time for others. Do not let the ways of the world crowd out this Christian virtue. Hospitality is a ministry.

The Bible is full of examples of women who cared for others. Consider Rahab of Jericho. She was not born into God's people. She had lived a sinful life. But when the two Israelite spies came to her city, she hid them on her rooftop and protected them. She confessed her faith in the God of Israel. By her courageous hospitality, she saved her entire household when Jericho fell. And she married Salmon, became the mother of Boaz, the great-grandmother of King David, and an ancestor of Jesus Christ Himself. A woman with a compassionate heart, even if her past is not clean, can become a mother in the line of the Messiah.

Consider the widow of Zarephath in First Kings chapter seventeen. During a terrible famine, the prophet Elijah came to her door and asked for water and bread. She replied that she had only a handful of meal and a little oil left, and was preparing to make a last meal for herself and her son before they died. Yet at Elijah's word, she shared what little she had. And the miracle began.

The barrel of meal did not waste, and the cruse of oil did not fail, for many days. When you give what you have to the Lord and His servants, God multiplies it. Do not say, "I have nothing to give."

Give what you have, and watch what the Lord will do.

Consider the Shunammite woman again, in Second Kings chapter four. She noticed the prophet Elisha passing through her town. She invited him to eat. She recognized him as a man of God. She went so far as to build a small room on her roof for him, so that he could rest whenever he came through. Because of her faithful hospitality, God gave her a son when she was childless, and even raised that son from the dead when he later died. A woman who opens her home to the servants of God will never lack God's blessing.

Consider Mary and Martha in Bethany. Their home was a place where Jesus Himself felt welcomed and loved. Martha served with great energy. Mary sat at His feet and learned from Him. Jesus loved to come to their home. He stayed with them. He ate with them. He wept at their brother's grave. And He raised Lazarus from the dead. Their hospitality opened the door for one of the greatest miracles in all of scripture. What miracle might God do in your home, if you opened it up to Him?

Consider Dorcas again, who made clothes for widows. Consider Mary of Jerusalem in Acts chapter twelve, whose house was used as a meeting place for the early church. Consider Phoebe, the deaconess at Cenchrea, who was a succourer of many. Woman after woman, in page after page, the Bible honors those who cared for others.

Let me speak practically. How do you practice hospitality and compassion in your life today?

Open your home. You do not need a big house. You do not need fancy furniture. You do not need to serve a big meal. What you need is a welcoming heart. Invite someone from church to Sunday lunch — maybe a widow, or a young man who lives alone, or a visiting preacher, or a neighbor who is not yet a believer. Share what you have cooked. Pray before the meal. Let them see your family and feel the love of Christ in your home.

Visit the sick. Many people in our communities are sick — with malaria, with HIV, with cancer, with tuberculosis, with the ordinary illnesses of life. A visit from a Christian sister, with a word of prayer and perhaps a small gift of food or fruit, can be a tremendous encouragement.

When Jesus spoke of the judgment, He said, "I was sick, and ye visited me." When you visit the sick in His name, you are visiting the Lord Himself.

Remember the widows. Widows in our communities often face great struggles. They may lose their land. They may be cut off from family. They may feel forgotten. The Bible tells us that pure religion and undefiled before God is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction. Find a widow in your church. Visit her. Pray with her. Help her if you can. You will be blessed beyond what you give.

Care for orphans. Uganda and East Africa have many orphans — some because of HIV and AIDS, some because of war, some because of poverty. The Church of Jesus Christ should be the first to care for these children. You may not be able to adopt an orphan, but you can help. Sponsor a child's school fees if you are able. Visit a children's home. Pray for the children there. Bring clothes or food. Love them in the name of Jesus.

Reach out to the poor. You yourself may not have much. But there is almost always someone poorer than you. Share what you have. The widow at the temple gave two small coins, and Jesus said she had given more than all the rich. It is not the amount. It is the heart.

Welcome strangers to your church. When a new person comes to your fellowship, go and greet them. Welcome them. Ask their name. Invite them home for a meal. Many people have wandered away from churches because no one spoke to them when they came. Do not let this happen in your church.

Listen. Sometimes the greatest ministry you can offer is not food or money but the gift of a listening ear. A burdened sister may need someone to hear her story, someone to cry with her, someone to pray with her. Be that person.

Let me tell you about an African Christian who showed remarkable compassion. Mary Slessor, the Scottish missionary, whom we mentioned earlier, adopted many abandoned children in Nigeria.

At one point she had nine orphans living with her, children who would have died without her care.

She once wrote that a woman's love can heal almost anything. This is not sentimental exaggeration.

The love of a Christian woman, filled with the Holy Spirit, is a powerful healing force in a broken world.

A final thought. Hospitality and compassion have limits, and we must be wise. You cannot help everyone. You must first care for your own household. You must protect yourself and your family from those who would harm you. But within those limits, there is usually much more you could do than you are currently doing. Ask the Lord to show you one person, one family, one widow, one orphan, one neighbor that He wants you to pour into this season. Then give yourself to that ministry with joy.

A Prayer Father of mercies, give me a compassionate heart. Open my eyes to see those around me who are in need. Open my hands to give what I have. Open my home to those who need welcome. Open my lips to pray for the sick and the suffering. Help me to remember the widows and the orphans. Help me to love my neighbor as myself. Make me a channel of Your love in a broken world. In the name of Jesus, who had compassion on the multitudes, Amen.

fields.title: Serving in the Church: Your Calling in the Body of Christ
fields.body_html:
"I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Romans 16:1 (KJV) The Church of Jesus Christ is not a building. It is the body of Christ — a living, breathing fellowship of believers, made up of men and women, young and old, rich and poor, from every tribe and every language. The Lord Jesus loves the Church. He gave Himself for her. He is preparing her as a pure bride. And every believer has a place in this body, with a calling to serve.

Sister, you belong in the Church. You are not a passive member, coming only on Sundays to be fed. You are a living stone in the temple of God. You have spiritual gifts. You have a ministry.

The Bible says that to every believer, grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ. God has placed you in your local church for a reason.

Let us look at some of the women in the New Testament who served in the early church.

Phoebe, in Romans chapter sixteen, is described as a servant — the Greek word is diakonos, from which we get the word deacon. Paul is commending her to the Romans. He says she has been a succourer, a helper, of many, including Paul himself. She was trusted with carrying Paul's great letter to Rome. Think of it. The letter to the Romans — perhaps the greatest theological letter ever written — was likely delivered by the hand of a woman. Phoebe was a servant of the church.

Priscilla, whom we have already mentioned, served alongside her husband Aquila in multiple cities. They opened their home as a meeting place for the church. They taught the scriptures. They worked with Paul. Paul calls them his helpers in Christ Jesus, who laid down their own necks for his life.

Junia, also in Romans sixteen, is called "of note among the apostles" — which likely means she and her companion Andronicus were well known and highly regarded by the apostolic community.

She was a kinswoman of Paul and had been imprisoned with him. Here was a woman who suffered for the gospel and was deeply respected.

Mary of Rome is mentioned in Romans chapter sixteen as one who "bestowed much labor on us."

Much labor. We do not know exactly what she did, but we know she worked hard for the gospel.

Euodia and Syntyche, in Philippians chapter four, are said to have labored with Paul in the gospel.

Sadly, Paul also had to urge them to be of the same mind in the Lord, because they had some disagreement. Even godly women can fall into conflict, and we must beware of that. But the point is — they labored in the gospel alongside Paul.

The four daughters of Philip the evangelist prophesied, according to Acts chapter twenty-one. They had a ministry of speaking God's word.

The deaconesses and widows of the early Church had roles of prayer, teaching other women, caring for orphans and the sick, and ministering to the bodies and souls of other believers. Widows over the age of sixty, who had been the wife of one man, who had raised children, who had lodged strangers, who had washed the saints' feet, who had relieved the afflicted — these women were enrolled to serve the Church.

From the very beginning, women have been essential to the ministry of the Church. The Lord Jesus Himself was supported in His earthly ministry by a group of women who traveled with Him and provided for His needs — Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Susanna, and many others.

Now let me speak practically. How should you serve in your local church?

First, commit to a local church. In our time, many Christians have become consumers rather than members. They float from church to church. They watch sermons online but never join a fellowship. They attend when it pleases them and stay home when it does not. Sister, this is not the biblical pattern. Find a Bible-believing church. Make a commitment. Be faithful. Support the pastor and the leaders.

Second, discover your gifts. God has given spiritual gifts to every believer. Some have the gift of teaching. Some have the gift of hospitality. Some have the gift of encouragement. Some have the gift of administration. Some have the gift of mercy. Some have the gift of giving. Some have the gift of leadership. Ask yourself: What do I love to do for the Lord? What do others thank me for?

Where do I see God using me? Talk with your pastor, your women's leader, and your trusted friends. They may see gifts in you that you do not see yourself.

Third, serve where you are needed. There are many ministries in a local church, and many of them especially need women. The Sunday School ministry. The choir. The women's fellowship. The hospitality team. The prayer ministry. The visitation ministry. The cleaning of the church. The care of the pastor's family. The youth ministry. The counseling of young brides. The ministry to the sick and the grieving. Do not wait to be asked. Ask the leaders where you can help, and then give yourself to the work faithfully.

Fourth, support your pastor and his wife. They carry a great load. They pray for you. They study late into the night to prepare sermons. They visit the sick. They bury the dead. They counsel the troubled. Pray for them. Encourage them with kind words. Respect them. Bring them gifts of food or firewood if you can. If you are a pastor's wife yourself, find other pastors' wives for mutual encouragement, because it is a lonely calling.

Fifth, give generously. Whatever you can give, give gladly. The Lord loves a cheerful giver. Tithe as the scriptures teach. Give special offerings when the need is great. Support the missionaries.

Help those in need within the fellowship. Remember that God is no man's debtor — what you give, He will replace, and more besides.

Sixth, honor the unity of the body. Do not be one of those women who causes divisions in the church. Do not gossip about the pastor. Do not spread rumors about other members. Do not form cliques that exclude others. Do not leave the church the first time something does not go your way.

The body of Christ is held together by love and forbearance. Be one who brings people together, not one who drives them apart.

Seventh, let me add a word about submission to spiritual authority. The scriptures teach that we are to obey those who rule over us in the Lord, and to submit to them, for they watch for our souls.

This does not mean that pastors and church leaders are infallible. They are not. But when godly leaders are making decisions and providing direction for the church, receive their leadership gratefully. Do not set yourself up as a judge over every sermon and every policy. Trust the Lord to correct what needs to be corrected in His time.

Let me close this chapter with a reflection. In the East African Revival, one of the beautiful fruits was the sense of family in the church. Brothers and sisters truly became brothers and sisters. They confessed sins to one another. They carried each other's burdens. They rejoiced together and wept together. This is the kind of church God wants. Ask yourself — am I helping to create that kind of family in my church? Am I a woman who brings warmth, love, and faithful service to the body of Christ? If so, you are carrying on the legacy of Phoebe, Priscilla, Mary, and all the faithful women who have gone before.

A Prayer Lord Jesus, I thank You for Your Church, the body of Christ. Thank You for placing me in my local fellowship. Show me the gifts You have given me. Show me where I can serve.

Make me faithful in small things and in great. Help me to love my pastor, to support the leaders, to build up the other believers, and never to be a source of division. Use my hands, my time, my voice, my home, and my resources for the building of Your Kingdom. In Your mighty name, Amen.

fields.title: A Light to Your Community: Being a Role Model
fields.body_html:
"Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid. Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house. Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven."

Matthew 5:14-16 (KJV) You are being watched. Your neighbors are watching you. Your relatives are watching you. Your children are watching you. The young women in your church are watching you. The unbelievers in your village are watching you. The way you speak, the way you carry yourself, the way you respond to trouble, the way you treat your husband, the way you spend your money — all of it is being observed. This is not to make you anxious. It is to make you mindful. Your life is a testimony. You will either honor the name of Christ, or you will bring reproach on it. Every day, you preach a sermon with your life, whether you intend to or not.

The Lord Jesus said that we are the light of the world. He did not say, "You can be the light if you try hard." He said, "You are the light." If you belong to Christ, you carry His light into every room you enter, every conversation you have, every shop you visit, and every household you join. The question is not whether you will shine. The question is whether your shining will draw people to God or cause them to stumble.

Let me show you several women from scripture who shone brightly in their communities.

Consider Esther. She was a young Jewish woman taken into the harem of King Xerxes of Persia.

By God's providence, she was chosen to be queen. But a wicked man named Haman plotted to destroy all the Jews in the empire. Her uncle Mordecai sent word to her: "Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Esther, at the risk of her own life, approached the king uninvited and interceded for her people. Her courage, her wisdom, her godly character saved a nation. She used the position God gave her for His purposes.

Every one of us has been placed in a certain family, a certain neighborhood, a certain workplace, a certain church, a certain community. You are there for such a time as this. Do not waste your position.

Consider Ruth. She was a Moabite, a foreigner among the people of Israel. She could have been treated with suspicion. Instead, her godly character won her the respect of the entire town of Bethlehem. Boaz said to her, "All the city of my people doth know that thou art a virtuous woman."

All the city. They had watched her. They had watched how she worked in the fields. They had watched how she cared for her mother-in-law Naomi. They had watched her humility and her faithfulness. Her life preached louder than any sermon. And through her quiet witness, she became the great-grandmother of King David, and an ancestor of Jesus Christ.

Consider Lydia. When she came to faith in Philippi, she did not keep it to herself. Her whole household was baptized. She opened her home to Paul and the traveling ministers. The Philippian church was planted in her house. Her conversion rippled out into a whole community.

In our own land, we see the same pattern. When the gospel came to Uganda in the late 1800s, some of the earliest and most fearless witnesses were young converts in the royal court. When King Mwanga demanded that they deny Christ, they refused. Young men and boys were burned at Namugongo in 1886. Christian women who survived continued to witness. One of them was Sara Nalwanga, who lived to a great age and told the story of those early days to younger believers. The blood of the martyrs became the seed of the Church. And today, Uganda is sometimes called the Pearl of Africa in part because of the deep Christian heritage planted by those faithful witnesses.

A generation later, the East African Revival swept through Uganda, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Kenya. A central feature of the movement was "walking in the light" — an open, honest life where sin was confessed, reconciliation was sought, and purity of heart was guarded. Women were some of the most powerful witnesses. They would stand in meetings and testify to what God had done.

They would confess sins publicly — not dwelling on shameful details, but acknowledging the grace that had set them free. They would sing songs of victory in the Swahili and Luganda tongues.

And unbelievers, watching these transformed women, would say, "What has happened to her? I want what she has." That is being a light.

Let me speak practically about how you can be a role model in your community today.

First, be dependable. Keep your word. If you say you will be at the meeting, be there on time. If you say you will pay the loan, pay it. If you say you will help with the cooking, show up. A Christian woman who can be trusted is a rare and beautiful thing.

Second, be kind to everyone. Greet the neighbors. Smile at the children. Speak kindly to the taxi driver, the market seller, the watchman, the house worker. Do not be proud. Do not treat people differently because of their wealth or status. The Lord Jesus treated the poor and the rich, the educated and the uneducated, the respected and the outcast with the same love.

Third, be generous. When a neighbor is in need, help if you can. When a relative is struggling, share what you have. When the offering plate comes around, give cheerfully. When someone shares good news, rejoice with them. The world is full of tight hearts. Let yours be wide open.

Fourth, be honest in everything. Do not lie. Do not cheat. Do not give false weights at the market.

Do not pay a bribe. Do not accept a bribe. Do not steal electricity or water. Do not cut corners when your employer is not watching. A reputation for honesty is worth more than gold.

Fifth, be dignified. Dress modestly. Speak with self-control. Do not drink excessively. Do not be loud and quarrelsome. Do not entertain the gossip and vulgarity of the world. Carry yourself with the quiet confidence of a daughter of the King.

Sixth, share the gospel. If you are known as a loving, kind, dependable Christian, people will eventually ask what makes you different. When they do, be ready to tell them about Jesus. Peter said, "Be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." You do not need to be a preacher. You need to be a witness.

Seventh, love your enemies. There will be people who dislike you. There will be neighbors who mistreat you. There will be family members who gossip against you. There will be perhaps even people in the church who stir up trouble. Do not repay evil for evil. Bless those who curse you.

Pray for those who spitefully use you. This is one of the hardest commands of our Lord, but it is one of the most powerful witnesses in a dark world.

Eighth, let your home be a witness. As we have said before, the home you keep — its peace, its order, its love, its hospitality — is a silent sermon that everyone who enters will receive.

Ninth, live with eternity in view. Remember that this world is not your home. You are passing through. The praise of men, the success of this life, the riches you accumulate — none of it comes with you to heaven. What matters is whether you have lived for Christ, loved others in His name, and been faithful to your calling. When you live with eternity in view, you live differently. You do not panic when trouble comes. You do not cling tightly to things that will pass away. You have peace because your treasure is in heaven, where neither moth nor rust corrupts.

Let your light shine, sister. Let it shine in your home, in your street, in your village, in your workplace, in your church, in your WhatsApp groups, in every place where God has placed you.

Do not hide it. Do not dim it out of fear of what others will think. A city on a hill cannot be hidden.

You are that city. The world is watching. Shine for the glory of your Father in heaven.

A Prayer Father, make me a light in my community. May my life point to Jesus. May my words carry Your truth. May my actions carry Your love. Forgive me for the times my light has been dim or hidden. Fill me afresh with Your Holy Spirit. Use me where You have placed me.

Let my family, my neighbors, and my community see You through me, and glorify You because of my witness. In the name of Jesus, the Light of the World, Amen.

fields.title: Knowing and Fellowshipping with God
fields.body_html:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.

Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."

Matthew 11:28-30 (KJV) We have come now to the final chapter of our journey together. We have spoken of many good and beautiful things — of prayer and the scriptures, of marriage and singleness, of raising children and managing homes, of working and teaching and serving and shining. All of these are precious callings. But if I left you with only these things, I would have failed you. Because none of them — not one — can be lived out in your own strength. The Christian life is not a long list of duties to perform. It is a living relationship with a living God. Everything else in this book flows from one great fountain: knowing and fellowshipping with God Himself. If you miss this, you miss everything. If you find this, you have found the one treasure that is more precious than all others.

Let me begin with the foundation of every other truth: You are loved. You are loved by the Living God, the Maker of heaven and earth. You are loved not because you have been good, not because you have prayed enough, not because you deserve it, not because you have pleased anyone. You are loved because love is who God is. The Bible says plainly that God is love. It is His very nature.

Long before you took your first breath, He knew you. Before He laid the foundation of the world, He chose you. On the cross, Jesus held you in His heart as He died for your sins. And right now, as you read these words, He is not frowning at you. He is not disappointed in you. He is smiling over you. The prophet Zephaniah says that the Lord your God rejoices over His people with singing. Jeremiah says He has loved you with an everlasting love. Paul says that nothing in all creation — not life, not death, not angels, not things present, not things to come, not height, not depth, not any other creature — shall be able to separate you from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Now hear this wonderful truth. The same God who loves you also wants to walk with you. He wants to share His life with you. From the very beginning, when sin had not yet entered the world, God walked with Adam and Eve in the garden in the cool of the day. That is His heart toward us.

When sin came, fellowship was broken — but through the precious blood of Jesus Christ it has been fully restored. Now, through the Holy Spirit, you can walk with God every day of your life.

You can know Him. You can hear His still small voice. You can be led by His gentle hand. You can share your joys and your sorrows with Him. Fellowship with God is not reserved for pastors or missionaries or people with special gifts. It is the birthright of every believer, and it is yours today.

Think of the people in scripture who walked closely with God. Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. Abraham was called the friend of God. Moses spoke with the Lord face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend. David was called a man after God's own heart.

Mary of Bethany sat at Jesus' feet and chose the good part, which would not be taken from her.

Paul said that one thing was his great longing — that he might know Him. These men and women are not far above you. They breathed the same air you breathe. They lived in the same kind of world. And the same God who met them is ready to meet you. The door is open. The invitation stands. Come.

Let us speak now of daily fellowship with the Lord. Like any good friendship, this fellowship grows through time spent together. I encourage you to set apart a time each day — even ten or fifteen minutes at first — simply to be with God. Open your Bible. Read a small portion. Meditate on what you read. Then speak to the Lord about what He has shown you. Thank Him. Confess sin if the Spirit brings something to mind. Ask His help for the day. Pour out your heart. Then be still, and listen. You may not hear a voice, but you will sense the gentle nudges of the Spirit. You will feel His peace settle over you. You will know that you are loved.

Do not let this time become a burden or a performance. Your Father is not grading you. He is delighted that you have come. When you miss a day, do not feel condemned — just come back the next day. When your heart is dry, come anyway. When your heart is full, come and praise Him.

Come as you are, every day, and slowly, over the weeks and years and decades, you will find that you have become a woman who walks with God. This is a great treasure. It is more valuable than gold. It will carry you through every season and every storm.

Our Lord Jesus gave us the most beautiful picture of fellowship in John chapter fifteen. He said, "I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit; for without me ye can do nothing." This is the great secret of the Christian life. Abiding in Christ. A branch does not struggle to bear fruit. It does not strain or sweat or work itself into exhaustion. It simply stays connected to the vine, and the life of the vine flows through it, and fruit comes naturally in its season. So with you, my sister. Stay connected to Jesus. Abide in His love.

Abide in His word. Abide in His presence. And the fruit will come — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. You cannot produce this fruit by striving. You can only receive it as the life of Christ flows through you.

Now let me speak of the Holy Spirit, for He is the One who makes this fellowship real and daily in your life. The Spirit is not a vague force or a distant influence. He is a person — the third person of the Trinity — who lives inside every true believer in Jesus Christ. On the day you believed, He came to dwell within you, and He will never leave. Jesus called Him the Comforter, which means one called alongside to help. He is your Helper, your Teacher, your Guide, your Strengthener, your Comforter in sorrow, your Convicter in sin, your Witness that you belong to God. When you do not know how to pray, He intercedes for you with groanings which cannot be uttered. When you are tempted, He gives you power to overcome. When you are confused, He leads you into truth.

When you are weary, He refreshes you. When you are afraid, He brings peace. He is the seal of God upon your life, the pledge of your eternal inheritance.

Walking in the Spirit simply means living with Him consciously, moment by moment. In the morning, when you rise, invite Him to lead you through the day: "Holy Spirit, fill me afresh. Guide my steps. Use my words." When you face a decision, pause and ask Him: "Holy Spirit, what would You have me do?" When you feel anger rising, whisper, "Holy Spirit, give me Your patience."

When you must speak a hard truth, ask Him for the right words. When you are going to visit the sick, ask Him to minister through you. When you are tempted, cry out to Him, and He will give you the way of escape. This is not complicated. It is the most natural thing in the world for a believer. Moment by moment, you walk in step with the Spirit, and He bears fruit through you that no human effort could ever produce. He does the work. You simply yield.

Now hear the wonderful words of our Lord in Matthew chapter eleven, which opened this chapter: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.

For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light." Consider what a yoke is. In our villages and on our farms, you have seen two oxen yoked together for plowing. A yoke is a wooden frame that joins them so that they pull together as one. When Jesus says, "Take my yoke upon you," He is inviting you to be joined to Him, to walk with Him, to work alongside Him. And here is the glory of it: He is the strong one. He does the heavy pulling. You only have to walk with Him, in step with Him, matching His pace, following His direction. That is why His yoke is easy and His burden is light.

The Christian life becomes heavy and crushing only when we try to pull alone. When we walk yoked to Jesus, His strength carries us, and even the hardest work becomes a joy.

This is why the Lord Jesus said that the first and greatest commandment is to love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind, and with all your strength. Loving God is not drudgery. It is the most joyful thing in all the universe. It is the reason you were made.

And how do you grow to love God more? The Bible gives us the answer: "We love him, because he first loved us." Your love for God is not something you must manufacture by hard effort. It grows as you see more and more how much He has loved you. So gaze upon His love. Meditate on the cross. Remember how He sought you when you were far from Him. Remember every answered prayer. Remember every tender mercy. Remember that He is carrying you even now, in this very moment. The more you see His love, the more your heart will swell with love for Him in return. You will find yourself singing to Him as you cook. You will find yourself thanking Him as you walk. You will find yourself delighting in Him in the middle of the ordinary day.

And then, out of that great love, flows the second great commandment — to love your neighbour as yourself. You cannot love others in your own strength. You will try, and you will fail, and you will grow weary, and you will become resentful. But when you are filled with the love of God, love for others pours out of you as naturally as water from a spring. You find yourself caring for the widow, kind to the stranger, patient with the difficult neighbour, tender with your children, gentle with your husband, forgiving to those who have wounded you. This is not because you have tried harder. It is because the Spirit of the Lord is producing His fruit in you. Love begets love.

This is the beautiful cycle of the Christian life: God loves you, you love Him back, and His love flows through you to everyone around you.

Let me tell you of a humble Frenchman named Brother Lawrence, who lived in the 1600s and worked in the kitchen of a monastery, washing pots and pans. He was not an educated man. He was not a great preacher. But he practiced what he called the presence of God in every small task.

Whether he was scrubbing a pot or picking up a straw from the floor, he did it with love for God and in quiet conversation with Him. Years after his death, his simple letters were gathered into a little book that has blessed Christians around the world for more than three hundred years. His great secret was that you do not need a special place or a special hour to walk with God. You can walk with Him in the kitchen, in the garden, at the market, on the road to fetch water, at the bedside of a sick child, in the quiet of the night when the house is asleep. The whole of life becomes worship when Christ is with you. This is also the great message of the East African Revival — a simple, daily, transparent walk with Jesus, keeping short accounts with Him and with others, living in the light.

My dear sister, as we close this chapter and this book, I want you to know, deep down in your soul, that the God who made the heavens loves you with an everlasting love. He is with you. His Spirit lives within you. His Son walks beside you, yoked to you, pulling the heavy part of every load.

The Father rejoices over you with singing. You are not alone. You are not forgotten. You are not forsaken. You are His beloved daughter, and He will never let you go. Walk with Him all your days. Love Him with your whole heart. Love your neighbour as yourself. Let your life become a quiet song of praise to the One who redeemed you. And when at last your journey on this earth is ended, you shall see Him face to face, and you shall hear the sweetest words ever spoken to a human heart: "Well done, good and faithful servant. Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord."

A Prayer Father of mercies, I come to You now with a heart wide open. Thank You for loving me with an everlasting love. Thank You for sending Your Son Jesus to die for me and to rise again that I might be Yours forever. Thank You for the gift of Your Holy Spirit, who lives within me. Draw me deeper into fellowship with You. Teach me to walk with You every hour of every day. Let me hear Your voice, feel Your presence, and know Your peace. Yoke me to Jesus, that His strength may carry me when I am weak. Fill me afresh with Your Spirit, that His fruit may grow in my life. Help me to love You with my whole heart, with my whole soul, with my whole mind, and with all my strength. And out of that love, help me to love my neighbour as myself. Make my life a song of praise to You. And when my days on this earth are ended, bring me home to see Your face. In the precious and wonderful name of Jesus Christ my Lord, Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion A Call to Action and a Closing Prayer
fields.body_html:
My beloved sister, we have come to the end of our journey through these pages, but in one sense, your journey is just beginning. You have read, you have considered, you have perhaps been challenged, encouraged, or convicted. Now the question becomes — what will you do?

The Bible says that faith without works is dead. The apostle James warns against being a hearer of the word only and not a doer, comparing such a person to one who looks in a mirror and immediately forgets what she saw. Do not let this book be a mirror you glance in and then forget.

Let it be a map you use, a tool you pick up again and again.

Let me leave you with a call to action, in the form of fourteen commitments you can make before God. They correspond to the fourteen chapters you have read. Take them to heart. Pray through them. Write them down. And ask the Lord to make you the woman He has called you to be.

Commit, first, to build your identity on Christ alone. Not on your husband, not on your children, not on your job, not on the opinions of others — but on the Rock of Jesus Christ.

Commit, second, to become a woman of prayer. Set a time, set a place, and begin today. Pray for your husband, your children, your pastor, your church, your village, and your nation.

Commit, third, to read and memorize the scriptures. Begin with small portions, but begin today.

Hide God's word in your heart.

Commit, fourth, to love and respect your husband with a Christ-like love. If you are unmarried, prepare your heart and character for the marriage God may be bringing. If you are widowed, cherish the good, and receive God's grace for the present. If you feel called to a single life, commit yourself to following and relying on God wholeheartedly.

Commit, fifth, to flourish in whatever season God has placed you in — single, married, waiting, or widowed. Remember that no Christian is truly alone. You have been given a great family in the Church, and your life, in any season, can bear much fruit for the Kingdom.

Commit, sixth, to nurture the next generation. Pour into the children in your life. Teach them the scriptures. Pray with them. Love them with both tenderness and wise discipline.

Commit, seventh, to manage your household with wisdom. Build your home and do not tear it down. Make it a place of peace, order, and welcome.

Commit, eighth, to teach other women and children. Receive from older sisters in the Lord. Pour into younger sisters. Help pass the faith to the next generation.

Commit, ninth, to guard your heart, your emotions, and your tongue. Ask the Holy Spirit daily to fill you with a meek and quiet spirit.

Commit, tenth, to work hard and to set godly goals. Use the abilities God has given you. Do not bury your talents.

Commit, eleventh, to care for others. Open your home. Visit the sick. Remember the widow and the orphan. Be a channel of the compassion of Christ.

Commit, twelfth, to serve in your local church. Find your place. Give your gifts. Honor your leaders. Build up the body of Christ.

Commit, thirteenth, to be a light in your community. Live so that those who watch you see Jesus.

Commit, fourteenth, and above all, to know and love the Lord your God with your whole heart.

Walk with Him daily. Abide in Christ. Rely on the Holy Spirit. Take His yoke, which is easy, and His burden, which is light. For out of this fellowship, every other calling finds its strength, its joy, and its meaning.

Now, my sister, these commitments are not fourteen heavy burdens to carry. They are fourteen ways to live out the one great calling to love God and love your neighbour. They are fourteen paths that all lead to the same destination — the joy of knowing Christ and making Him known.

You may feel overwhelmed. You may feel inadequate. You may feel tired. You may feel, "I cannot do all of this." You are right. You cannot. But the Holy Spirit can work through you to do all of this and more. The same Spirit who empowered Deborah to lead armies, who gave Esther courage to approach the king, who filled Mary to bear the Son of God, who sent Priscilla and Aquila as partners in the gospel, who lit the fires of revival in the hills of Rwanda and Uganda — that same Spirit lives in you. You are not alone. The God who began a good work in you is faithful to complete it. He will not leave you or forsake you. He has equipped you for every good work He has prepared for you.

Go forth, my sister, in the strength of the Lord. The world needs Christian women more than ever — women who pray, who nurture, who teach, who work, who love, who serve, who shine. Your generation is waiting for you to take your place. Your children are waiting to be shaped by your hands. Your nation is waiting for the mothers and grandmothers who will call down the power of God from heaven.

And one day, when your race is finished and your course is done, you will hear those blessed words from the lips of the Lord Jesus — "Well done, thou good and faithful servant. Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord." That joy awaits every daughter of God who has been faithful. It is worth every tear, every prayer, every labor, every sacrifice.

A Closing Prayer Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, I come before You today as Your daughter.

I thank You that You made me. I thank You that You saved me. I thank You that You are shaping me into the woman You have called me to be. I confess that I have fallen short in many ways. I have not always prayed as I should. I have not always loved as I should. I have not always walked as I should. Forgive me by the blood of Jesus. Wash me clean.

Renew a right spirit within me. Fill me afresh with Your Holy Spirit. Teach me to walk in the good works You have prepared for me. Help me to love my husband and children. Help me to teach the next generation. Help me to manage my home with wisdom. Help me to work with strength and integrity. Help me to serve Your Church faithfully. Help me to be a light in my community. Clothe me with strength and dignity, that I may laugh at the days to come. Give me grace for today and hope for tomorrow. And when this earthly journey is over, receive me into Your everlasting kingdom, where I shall see You face to face with all the saints. I ask all of this in the name of Jesus Christ, my Lord and Saviour, who lives and reigns with You and the Holy Spirit, one God, forever and ever. Amen.

To God be the glory! Hallelujah!
